Every director discloses his concern or interest in any company, body corporate, firm or association of individuals at the first board meeting he attends in a financial year, and again on any change — a duty owed regardless of the size of the interest. Separately, an interested director discloses that interest in a specific contract or arrangement and does not participate in the board's discussion or vote on it; a contract entered in breach is voidable at the company's option.

concepts.subsection: Contract of employment with managing or whole-time director — section 190
concepts.statement: A company keeps at its registered office a copy of its managing or whole-time director's contract of service, or a written memorandum of its terms where the contract is not in writing, open for inspection by members without charge during business hours — a members' right the board or the company secretary cannot narrow to itself or to the auditor.

A company with one or more subsidiaries, including associate companies and joint ventures, prepares a consolidated financial statement in addition to its standalone statements, in the same form and manner, following the applicable accounting standards, and lays it before the annual general meeting alongside the standalone statements. Consolidation covers every subsidiary; it is not a management choice of which ones to fold in.

The board's report states, among other prescribed particulars, a director's responsibility statement under section 134(5), particulars of loans, guarantees and investments under section 186, particulars of related-party contracts in the prescribed form, the CSR policy and initiatives, and — for listed and other prescribed companies — a statement on the formal annual evaluation of the board, its committees and individual directors. These are matters the report must itself state, not particulars merely available on request.

concepts.subsection: Annual return and its certification — section 92
concepts.statement: Every company files its annual return within sixty days of the annual general meeting, or of the date by which the AGM should have been held where none took place, with reasons for the default. Beyond the prescribed size thresholds, and for every listed company, the return additionally carries certification by a company secretary in practice rather than an in-house signature alone.

citation.ref: Section 92, read with the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014

concepts.statement: A rights issue offer goes to existing equity shareholders in proportion to their holding, stays open for not less than fifteen days and not more than thirty days, and carries a right of renunciation in favour of another person unless the articles exclude it. The board cannot allot before the offer period lapses or ahead of renunciation choices being exercised or declined.

concepts.subsection: Debentures — trustee and redemption reserve, section 71
concepts.statement: A company issuing debentures at the prescribed scale appoints a debenture trustee and executes a debenture trust deed before making the offer, so that an independent party holds the security and enforces the debenture-holders' rights — the issuer's own guarantee is not a substitute for that independent office. Certain classes of debenture issuer must additionally build a debenture redemption reserve out of profits, though this requirement has been narrowed for some classes over successive amendments.

On admission of a corporate insolvency resolution application, the adjudicating authority declares a moratorium barring institution or continuation of suits against the corporate debtor, transfer or disposal of its assets, enforcement of any security interest, and recovery of property by an owner or lessor in the debtor's possession; supply of essential goods and services to the debtor cannot be terminated during this period. The moratorium does not extend to a surety in a contract of guarantee for the corporate debtor.

concepts.subsection: Going concern across FR and audit
concepts.statement: Material uncertainties about going concern are disclosed in the financial statements themselves — Ind AS 1 requires it of management when it is aware of them. A mention in the board's report or a covering letter is not a substitute, and the auditor's going concern section points to the note, so the note must exist.

concepts.subsection: Related party transactions under company law
concepts.statement: A contract with a related party of the kinds listed in section 188 — sale or purchase of goods, property, services, agency — needs board approval by resolution when it is not in the ordinary course of business or not at arm's length, and shareholder approval past the prescribed thresholds. An interested director does not participate.

A chartered accountant in practice cannot charge professional fees as a percentage of profits or contingent on results, outside the specific exceptions the Council has carved out — an auditor paid a share of what he certifies has bought a stake in the number.

concepts.subsection: Fraud reporting under the Companies Act
concepts.statement: An auditor who has reason to believe a fraud of one crore rupees or more is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees reports it to the Central Government, routed first through the board or audit committee for their reply within the prescribed time. Frauds below that threshold go to the board or audit committee, and are disclosed in the board's report.

A company crossing any one threshold — net worth ₹500 crore, turnover ₹1000 crore, or net profit ₹5 crore in the immediately preceding year — must constitute a CSR committee and spend 2 per cent of its average net profits of the three preceding years. Unspent amounts follow the ongoing-project rules or move to a specified fund; mere disclosure no longer discharges it.

concepts.subsection: Internal financial controls in the auditor's report
concepts.statement: The auditor of a company reports on whether the company has an adequate internal financial controls system with reference to financial statements and whether it operated effectively — a separate opinion under section 143(3)(i), distinct from the opinion on the statements themselves. Smaller private companies are exempted by notification.

A chartered accountant in practice may not solicit clients or professional work directly or indirectly — by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview. Responding to tenders, applying for empanelment that has been announced, and seeking work from another chartered accountant in practice sit outside the bar.

The audit committee of a listed public company needs a minimum of three directors, with independent directors forming a majority, and a majority of members — the chairperson included — able to read and understand financial statements. It recommends auditor appointment and remuneration, reviews independence, and runs the vigil mechanism.

CARO 2020 applies to companies generally but not to banking companies, insurance companies, section 8 companies, one person companies, small companies, and private companies within all the prescribed size limits — paid-up capital and reserves up to one crore, borrowings up to one crore, and revenue up to ten crore. Cross any one limit and the order applies.

Dividend is declared out of profits after providing for depreciation, or out of free reserves under the prescribed conditions. Losses and depreciation of earlier years are set off first, and the securities premium and revaluation surplus are not distributable — a dividend needs earned, realised profit behind it.

Listed companies and the prescribed classes cannot appoint an individual auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, or an audit firm for more than two such terms, followed in each case by a five-year cooling-off. A firm sharing common partners with the retiring firm is caught by the same bar.

Internal audit is compulsory for every listed company, and for unlisted public companies and private companies crossing the prescribed size lines — for a private company, turnover of two hundred crore rupees or outstanding borrowings of one hundred crore during the preceding year. The internal auditor may be a chartered accountant, cost accountant, or other professional the board decides, and may be an employee.

A listed public company needs at least one-third of its board as independent directors. An independent director holds office for up to five years a term, at most two consecutive terms, then a three-year cooling-off during which no association with the company is permitted. Independence is defined by negatives — no pecuniary relationship with the company beyond permitted limits, no promoter linkage, and the director must declare independence at first appointment and annually.

A company's loans, guarantees, securities and investments beyond sixty per cent of paid-up capital plus free reserves and securities premium — or one hundred per cent of free reserves plus securities premium, whichever is more — need a special resolution. Every such loan needs prior approval of all directors present at the board meeting, carries interest at no less than the prevailing government-security yield, and is barred entirely while the company is in default on public deposits.

A company may not lend to, or guarantee or secure the debts of, its directors or their partners and firms — that circle is absolute. One ring out — a private company in which a director is interested, or a body corporate under a director's control — the loan is possible, but only with a special resolution and the borrower using it for its principal business. Loans to managing or whole-time directors ride narrow exceptions such as a scheme for all employees.

An operational creditor must serve a demand notice under section 8 before filing; the corporate debtor has ten days to point to a pre-existing dispute or proof of payment, and a genuine pre-existing dispute kills the section 9 application — insolvency is not a debt recovery forum. A financial creditor under section 7 faces no such dispute defence; default alone carries the application.

Prescribed companies must have whole-time key managerial personnel — a managing director or CEO or manager (or in their absence a whole-time director), a company secretary, and a chief financial officer. A whole-time KMP holds office in only one company at a time (a subsidiary excepted), and a vacancy must be filled by the board within six months.

concepts.subsection: Oppression and mismanagement — who may apply
concepts.statement: A petition under section 241 needs standing under section 244: for a company with share capital, at least one hundred members, or one-tenth of the total members, or holders of one-tenth of the issued share capital — whichever is least — with all calls paid. The Tribunal may waive the threshold for a deserving case, and consenting members can combine to make up the numbers.

A buy-back may not exceed twenty-five per cent of paid-up capital plus free reserves, with the board alone able to approve up to ten per cent of paid-up equity plus free reserves and a special resolution needed beyond; post buy-back debt may not exceed twice the capital and free reserves; shares must be fully paid; and a year must pass between buy-backs. Funding comes from free reserves, securities premium or fresh issue proceeds of other securities.

A private placement offer goes to identified persons only — at most two hundred in a financial year, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employee stock options — with no public advertisement, application money through banking channels into a separate account, allotment within sixty days or refund, and no use of the money before allotment and filing. Breach of the public-solicitation bar converts the issue into a deemed public offer with all its consequences.

A charge on company property must be registered within thirty days of creation, with the Registrar able to allow late filing on payment of ad valorem fees within the extended statutory window. An unregistered charge is void against the liquidator and other creditors — the debt survives and becomes immediately payable, but the lender queues as unsecured when it mattered most. Registration is the charge-holder's protection and may be filed by the lender itself if the company defaults on filing.

Every listed company — and public companies above the prescribed size lines of paid-up capital or turnover — annexes a secretarial audit report from a practising company secretary to the board's report, covering compliance with the Companies Act, securities laws and other laws applicable to the company. The board must respond to every qualification in the report; the auditor here is a company secretary in practice, not a chartered accountant.

The first AGM is held within nine months of the first financial year's close; every later AGM within six months of the financial year's end, with no more than fifteen months between two AGMs. The Registrar may extend a later AGM by up to three months for special reasons — never the first. Business hours, a non-national-holiday day, and the registered office's city frame where and when it happens.

concepts.subsection: Strike off and restoration — sections 248 and 252
concepts.statement: The Registrar may strike off a company that never commenced business or has not operated for two financial years without dormant status — after notice and a chance to respond — and a company may apply for strike off itself after clearing its liabilities. Restoration runs through the Tribunal: an aggrieved person appeals within three years, and the company, a member, creditor or workman may apply within twenty. Liability of directors and members survives the striking off as if the company continued.

The board, if the articles authorise, may appoint an additional director who holds office only up to the next annual general meeting — or the date by which that AGM should have been held, so delaying the meeting cannot extend the seat. A person who fails to get appointed as a director in a general meeting cannot come in as an additional director. Regularisation at the AGM converts the seat into an ordinary directorship.

A small company is a non-public company with paid-up capital up to four crore rupees and turnover up to forty crore — never a holding or subsidiary company, a section 8 company, or one governed by a special Act. The status buys lighter compliance: no cash flow statement, an abridged annual return signable by a director alone, two board meetings a year in place of four, no auditor rotation, and lighter penalties under the Act's small-company provisions.

Small companies, a holding company with its wholly owned subsidiary, and other prescribed classes may merge without the Tribunal: notice to the Registrar and Official Liquidator for objections, member approval by ninety per cent of total shares and creditor approval by ninety per cent in value, then registration of the scheme by the Central Government (the Regional Director). If objections raise substance, the Regional Director may refer the scheme to the Tribunal — the fast track can slow down, but it starts without a court.

Once the Central Government assigns a company's affairs to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office, no other investigating agency under the Companies Act proceeds with the same matter, and pending investigations transfer to SFIO. SFIO officers hold arrest powers for the fraud offence under section 447, which is cognizable for that purpose, with bail conditioned on the twin tests. Its report can found prosecution as if it were a police report.

A company may accept deposits from its members by resolution with the prescribed conditions; accepting deposits from the public is reserved to eligible companies — public companies with net worth of at least one hundred crore rupees or turnover of at least five hundred crore — with credit rating, deposit repayment reserve and the rest. Amounts from directors (declared as own funds) and many commercial receipts are excluded from "deposit"; on default, depositors reach the Tribunal, and fraudulent acceptance attracts personal liability.

Listed and prescribed public companies constitute a nomination and remuneration committee of three or more non-executive directors, at least half independent; the chairperson of the company may sit on it but may not chair it. The committee identifies candidates, evaluates performance, and frames the remuneration policy the board discloses. Its recommendations discipline board appointments the way the audit committee disciplines the accounts.

Every listed company — and companies that accept public deposits or have borrowed more than fifty crore rupees from banks and financial institutions — must operate a vigil mechanism for directors and employees to report genuine concerns, with safeguards against victimisation and direct access to the audit committee's chairperson in appropriate or exceptional cases. Its existence is disclosed on the website and in the board's report.

A public company's total managerial remuneration caps at eleven per cent of net profits — within it, five per cent for one managing or whole-time director, ten per cent for all of them together, and one per cent (or three where no managing director exists) for other directors. Exceeding a limit needs a special resolution — Central Government approval was abolished in 2018 — and in a no-profit year, Schedule V's slabs by effective capital govern instead. Excess drawn without authority is held in trust and recovered, unless the company waives it by special resolution.

An Input Service Distributor is an office of the supplier that receives tax invoices for input services and distributes the credit to its other registered units — distinct persons of the same legal entity — by issuing an ISD invoice. Distribution runs pro rata to the turnover of each recipient unit in the relevant period, eligible and ineligible credit are kept apart, and the distributor can never distribute more credit than is available for the period.

concepts.subsection: Rule 42 — Reversal of ITC on inputs and input services
concepts.statement: Where inputs and input services are used partly for taxable or business supplies and partly for exempt supplies or non-business purposes, credit attributable exclusively to the exempt or non-business use is reversed in full at the outset. The remaining common credit — used for both — is reversed monthly by a formula keyed to the ratio of exempt turnover to total turnover, and the reversal is trued up once a year against the actual annual figures.

concepts.subsection: Section 18(6) — ITC on capital goods, disposal before useful life
concepts.statement: Credit on capital goods is available in full at the time of receipt, without the staggering that the earlier VAT regime used. If capital goods on which credit was taken are later supplied outward, the registered person must pay an amount equal to the credit taken reduced by the prescribed percentage points for each quarter of use, or the tax on the transaction value of that supply — whichever of the two is higher. Disposal claws back whatever share of the credit the period of use has not yet earned.

concepts.subsection: QRMP scheme — quarterly return, monthly payment
concepts.statement: A registered person whose aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year stays within the notified threshold may opt to file GSTR-3B quarterly while still paying tax every month, using either a fixed sum linked to the previous quarter's cash payment or self-assessment for the first two months. Invoices for those first two months can be uploaded through the Invoice Furnishing Facility so recipients still see credit without waiting for the quarterly return.

Every registered person, other than the specified exceptions such as a casual taxable person, a non-resident taxable person, an Input Service Distributor and persons subject to TDS or TCS, must furnish an annual return for the financial year on or before the thirty-first of December following its end. The annual return reconciles the year's periodic returns; it is a summary instrument, not a fresh assessment.

concepts.subsection: Sections 73 and 74 — Demands, fraud vs bona fide
concepts.statement: Section 73 governs tax short-paid, unpaid, wrongly refunded, or credit wrongly availed or utilised, for reasons other than fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression — with a lighter penalty and real concessions for paying before or soon after the show-cause notice. Section 74 covers the identical shortfalls where fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression is present, carrying a longer limitation period and a materially higher penalty. The line between the two is the presence of dishonesty, not the size of the shortfall.

concepts.subsection: Section 107 — Appeal to the Appellate Authority, pre-deposit
concepts.statement: An appeal to the first Appellate Authority is not entertained unless the appellant has paid the full amount admitted as due, plus ten per cent of the remaining disputed tax. This pre-deposit is what buys a stay on recovery of the balance disputed amount while the appeal is pending — it is a precondition to the appeal being heard at all, not a discretionary figure an officer can vary.

A taxable person unable to determine the value of a supply or the applicable rate of tax may request provisional assessment, executing a bond with security for the differential tax. The proper officer must finalise the assessment ordinarily within six months, extendable, and interest on any additional tax found due at finalisation runs from the original due date for payment of that tax, not from the date of the final order.

concepts.subsection: Section 36 — Period of retention of accounts
concepts.statement: Every registered person must retain the accounts and records section 35 requires for seventy-two months from the due date of furnishing the annual return for the year they relate to. A registered person who is party to an appeal, revision or any other proceeding, or under investigation, must keep the relevant records for a further year after the proceeding's final disposal, or to the seventy-two-month mark, whichever is later.

Goods deposited in a licensed customs warehouse under a warehousing bond remain there without payment of duty until an ex-bond bill of entry is filed for home consumption or the goods are re-exported. Ordinary warehoused goods draw interest on the duty once they overstay the interest-free period the Customs Act allows, and the rate of duty and valuation for the eventual clearance are taken on the date of the ex-bond bill of entry, not the date of warehousing.

An Indian resident, or a foreigner residing in India, returning from a country other than Nepal, Bhutan or Myanmar gets a General Free Allowance covering new articles up to a notified value without payment of duty. Used personal effects — worn clothing, a used laptop and the like — sit outside the definition of dutiable articles altogether, so they travel free of that value ceiling; the allowance is tested only against genuinely new purchases.

concepts.subsection: Section 27 — Casual taxable person, registration validity
concepts.statement: A casual taxable person must apply for registration at least five days before commencing business and deposit an amount equal to the estimated tax liability for the period of registration, as advance tax. The certificate of registration is valid for the period specified in the application or ninety days from the effective date of registration, whichever is earlier, and it may be extended by a further period not exceeding ninety days.

Input tax credit needs every section 16(2) condition together — a tax invoice, receipt of the goods or services, the detail appearing in GSTR-2B, the tax actually paid to the Government by the supplier, and the return filed. Holding a valid invoice while the supplier has not paid the tax defeats the credit.

For notified supplies — legal services from an advocate to a business entity among them — the recipient, not the supplier, is liable to pay the tax, and pays it in cash rather than through input tax credit.

Registration becomes compulsory when aggregate turnover crosses ₹20 lakh for a supplier of services. The ₹40 lakh limit is for suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States, and special category States carry lower limits.

A composition taxpayer cannot make inter-State outward supplies of goods. The scheme trades a small turnover-based levy for staying local; crossing the State line with outward supplies forfeits eligibility.

Additions to the transaction value of imported goods include selling commissions, and cost of transport and insurance to the place of importation — but buying commission, paid to the importer's own agent for representing him abroad, is not added.

concepts.subsection: Section 16(4) — Time limit for input tax credit
concepts.statement: Input tax credit for an invoice cannot be taken after the thirtieth of November following the end of the financial year the invoice belongs to, or the filing of the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier. A valid, eligible credit dies purely of lateness.

concepts.subsection: IGST Act — Place of supply of goods
concepts.statement: Where a supply involves movement of goods, the place of supply is the location where the movement terminates for delivery to the recipient. Who arranges the transport does not decide it; where the goods end up does.

An advance received for a supply of services is taxable when received. For goods, suppliers other than composition taxpayers pay tax only on issue of the invoice — advances for goods were taken out of the tax net by notification. The same rupee of advance is taxed on one side of the goods-services line and not the other.

A discount given after the supply reduces the taxable value only if it was agreed before or at the time of supply and can be linked to the specific invoices, and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit. A goodwill discount invented after the event changes the price, not the tax.

Interest on delayed payment of tax runs at 18 per cent, and on the portion paid through the electronic cash ledger it is charged only on that net cash amount where the return is filed late — the credit-covered portion carries no interest. Wrongly availed and utilised credit draws its own interest.

Inputs sent for job work must return, or be supplied from the job worker's premises, within one year; capital goods within three years. Miss the window and the original despatch is deemed a supply from the day the goods went out, with tax and interest reaching back to it.

Exports and supplies to SEZ units are zero-rated, not exempt: the output carries no tax, yet input tax credit survives. The exporter either supplies under a letter of undertaking without paying tax and claims refund of unutilised credit, or pays IGST and claims refund of the tax paid.

An e-way bill is generated before movement of goods worth more than fifty thousand rupees in a consignment. The obligation attaches to the movement, not the sale — stock transfers, job work despatches and sales returns all need one, and some States set higher intra-State limits.

concepts.subsection: Section 129 — Detention of goods in transit
concepts.statement: Goods moved in contravention — typically without a valid e-way bill or invoice — are detained, and release requires a penalty of two hundred per cent of the tax payable where the owner comes forward. Detention is a transit consequence and runs independently of whether the tax on the supply itself was ever evaded.

Four transactions are supplies even without consideration — permanent transfer of business assets on which credit was taken, supplies between related or distinct persons in business, goods moved through agents who undertake to supply or receive on the principal's behalf, and imported services from a related person for business. Employer gifts to an employee stay out up to fifty thousand rupees a year.

concepts.subsection: Schedule III — Neither goods nor services
concepts.statement: Schedule III lists what GST cannot touch at all — an employee's services to the employer in the course of employment, sale of land and of completed buildings, actionable claims other than specified ones, funeral services, and duties of courts and MPs. These are not exempt supplies; they are not supplies, so they never enter aggregate turnover.

A refund claim is filed within two years from the relevant date, and the relevant date moves with the ground of the claim — export shipment dates for goods exported, the date payment lands for export of services, the judgment's date where tax was paid under a later-reversed demand. Miss the window and the money stays with the Government however good the ground was.

A supplier of services outside the restaurant category, ineligible for the ordinary composition scheme, may opt for the special scheme where aggregate turnover in the preceding year stayed within fifty lakh rupees, paying six per cent. The ordinary scheme's goods-centred gates do not decide this one.

Input tax credit on motor vehicles for transporting persons with seating capacity up to thirteen (including the driver) is blocked — unless the vehicle is used for further supply of such vehicles, transporting passengers, or driving training. Vehicles above thirteen seats and goods-transport vehicles are outside the block, and services of insurance, repair and maintenance follow the vehicle they attach to.

concepts.subsection: Section 13 — Time of supply of services
concepts.statement: For services, time of supply is the earlier of invoice and payment where the invoice issues within the thirty-day limit; where it does not, the earlier of the date the service is provided and the payment. The clock decides which tax period the liability lands in — issuing the invoice late does not push the liability later.

Section 74 refunds up to ninety-eight per cent of import duty when the imported goods themselves are re-exported within two years, identified as the same goods. Goods that were used before re-export get tapering rates by period of use. Section 75 is the other drawback — for duty on inputs consumed in manufacturing exported goods — and the two never apply to the same claim.

concepts.subsection: IGST — Place of supply for immovable property services
concepts.statement: Services directly relating to immovable property — architects, surveyors, engineers, hotel accommodation, letting, construction-linked services — are supplied where the property sits, whatever the locations of supplier and recipient. The property anchors the tax, and if it lies outside India the default recipient-location rule takes over.

concepts.subsection: Schedule II — Works contract as a service
concepts.statement: A works contract — a contract for building, construction, fabrication or similar work on immovable property involving transfer of property in goods — is deemed wholly a supply of services by Schedule II. One levy, one classification: the old VAT-plus-service-tax split of a single contract is gone, and works contract input credit has its own restrictions in section 17(5).

Customs duty is assessed on transaction value — the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India — plus prescribed additions, at the time and place of importation. A relationship between buyer and seller displaces that price only where it influenced it; a related-party price the importer shows to be at arm's length stands.

The value of supply includes taxes other than GST itself, amounts the supplier was liable to pay but the recipient paid, incidental expenses like packing and commission charged by the supplier, interest or penalty for delayed payment of consideration, and subsidies directly linked to price from anyone other than the Government. Each inclusion widens the base beyond the bare price.

A service is exported only when all five conditions hold: supplier in India, recipient outside India, place of supply outside India, payment received in convertible foreign exchange (or INR where RBI permits), and supplier and recipient not merely two establishments of one person. Failing any one, the supply is not an export and zero-rating is lost.

A supplier who has charged too much tax — goods returned, deficient supply, price revised down — issues a credit note and reduces output liability, but only up to the thirtieth of November following the financial year of supply (or the annual return, if earlier), and only if the incidence of tax has not been passed to someone who bears it. A commercial credit note without GST can issue any time, adjusting price but not tax.

Import of goods is taxed as inter-State supply, but the IGST is levied and collected as customs duty — under the Customs Tariff Act, on the value determined under the Customs Act at the point of importation, together with basic customs duty. The importer generally takes credit of the IGST so paid; basic customs duty is never creditable.

Registrations of one entity in different States are distinct persons, and supplies between them — stock transfers, services of one office to another — are taxable supplies even without consideration, valued under the rules with full input credit typically flowing. One legal person, several taxable persons: the design keeps each State's revenue whole.

Goods pilfered after unloading but before clearance attract no duty from the importer — unless restored — and the custodian pays instead; goods lost or destroyed before clearance earn remission on the Assistant Commissioner's satisfaction, and goods relinquished before clearance drop the duty too. Pilferage is automatic by the section's operation; remission must be sought and shown.

An e-commerce operator collects tax at source on the net value of supplies made through it by others — a collection mechanism, not a levy. For the notified services — passenger transport, accommodation, restaurants, housekeeping — section 9(5) goes further: the operator is liable to pay the tax as if it were the supplier, and the actual supplier's registration position changes accordingly. TCS and 9(5) never apply to the same supply.

Four different fates: a nil-rated supply is taxable at zero in the tariff; an exempt supply is freed by notification and includes nil-rated and non-taxable supplies for definition purposes; a non-taxable supply is outside the levy itself, like alcohol for human consumption; zero-rated means exports and SEZ supplies — taxable in principle, taxed at zero, with input credit preserved. Only zero-rating keeps the credit; exemption breaks the credit chain.

An advance ruling binds only the applicant who sought it and the jurisdictional officers in respect of that applicant — not other taxpayers, however identical their facts, and not other States' authorities. It holds unless law, facts or circumstances change, and a ruling obtained by fraud or suppression is void from the start. Other taxpayers may read it as persuasive weather, never as shelter.

Government departments, local authorities and notified entities deduct tax at source at two per cent from payments to suppliers where a contract's taxable value exceeds two and a half lakh rupees — the deduction tested contract-wise, on value excluding GST. No deduction where the supplier's State and the place of supply differ from the recipient's State. The deductee takes the amount as cash ledger credit, not as input tax.

concepts.subsection: Section 54(3) — Refund of unutilised input tax credit
concepts.statement: Accumulated input tax credit is refundable in exactly two cases: zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax, and the inverted duty structure — input tax rates exceeding output rates. Credit piling up because sales are slow, or because outputs are exempt, earns no refund; the inverted-structure refund runs on the rule's formula and excludes input services from the computation.

concepts.subsection: Customs — Date for rate of duty
concepts.statement: The rate of duty and tariff valuation for imports is taken on the date of filing the bill of entry for home consumption — or, for warehoused goods, the date of the ex-bond bill of entry when the goods leave the warehouse for home consumption. A rate change while goods sit in bond therefore lands on the importer; the vessel's arrival date matters only where the bill was filed in advance.

Certain persons register regardless of turnover: inter-State taxable suppliers of goods, persons liable under reverse charge, casual taxable persons with no fixed place in the State, non-resident taxable persons, e-commerce operators, TDS deductors, and agents supplying for others. The threshold exemption belongs to section 22; section 24's list overrides it — though inter-State suppliers of services enjoy a notified threshold relaxation the goods side never got.

The Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme imports capital goods at zero customs duty against an export obligation of six times the duty saved, to be discharged over six years from authorisation — with the goods installed and put to use, and the obligation over and above the average of past exports. Default surrenders proportionate duty with interest; the scheme buys machinery cheap with a promise, and the promise is enforced.

citation.ref: EPCG scheme (export obligation 6x duty saved in 6 years)

concepts.statement: Where goods are delivered to one person on the instruction of another, the law sees two supplies: supplier to the instructing buyer, and instructing buyer to the actual recipient — with the first leg's place of supply deemed to be the instructing buyer's principal place of business, wherever the goods physically went. Tax type on each leg follows its own deemed geography, and each leg carries its own invoice.

Tariff classification walks the General Interpretative Rules in order: headings and their notes first; incomplete articles classify as complete if they have the essential character; mixtures and composites classify by the material giving essential character; and only when goods remain equally classifiable under two headings does the later heading win. The specific description always beats the general one before any tie-breaker is reached.

concepts.subsection: Rule 32(5) — Margin scheme for second-hand goods
concepts.statement: A dealer in second-hand goods, selling them as such after at most minor processing that does not change their nature, may pay GST only on the margin — selling price less purchase price, with a negative margin ignored — provided no input tax credit was taken on the purchase. Buying from unregistered consumers is the scheme's habitat; take credit on the inward side and the whole selling price becomes taxable.

Costs a supplier incurs as a pure agent of the recipient stay out of the value of supply when every condition holds: the supplier contracts as the recipient's authorised agent for that payment, the recipient alone uses what was procured, the actual amount is separately indicated on the invoice and recovered without markup, and it is in addition to the supplier's own services. Mark it up, or bundle it, and the exclusion is gone.

A composite supply bundles naturally — two or more taxable supplies ordinarily supplied together with one principal supply — and takes the principal supply's rate. A mixed supply is an artificial bundle for a single price whose parts could be sold separately, and it takes the highest rate among them. Natural bundling is tested by trade practice: what buyers expect to come together.

Actionable claims are goods by definition, yet Schedule III keeps them outside GST — except the specified ones: lottery, betting, gambling, and since the 2023 amendments, online money gaming, which are taxable, valued on their own rules. An unsecured debt assigned, an insurance claim transferred — outside the levy; a lottery ticket sold — squarely inside it.

concepts.subsection: Section 50(3) — Interest on wrongly availed credit
concepts.statement: Interest on wrongly availed input tax credit runs only where the credit is also utilised — credit that sat unused in the electronic credit ledger until reversal costs nothing. The same mercy governs delayed payment interest under section 50(1): where the return is late but the tax was paid by balance in the cash ledger, interest applies on the portion paid through cash late, computed on the net cash liability. Both rules arrived as retrospective corrections of harsher readings.

A customs duty refund is paid to the claimant only on proof that the duty's incidence was not passed on to any other person; otherwise the refund is sanctioned but credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund. The presumption runs against the claimant — passing on is assumed until displaced by evidence such as a chartered accountant's certificate and unchanged prices. Captive consumption and duty paid under protest walk the same test.

Services imported for business bear IGST in the recipient's hands under reverse charge — the foreign supplier is beyond the levy's practical reach, so the Indian recipient self-assesses, pays in cash, and takes credit where eligible. Import by an individual for personal purposes stays outside as not being in the course of business — except OIDAR services, which are taxed even to consumers with the foreign supplier itself required to register.

Online information and database access or retrieval services — streaming, cloud storage, e-books, online advertising, essentially automated digital delivery with minimal human intervention — are taxed in India even when supplied to unregistered consumers. The foreign supplier (or its appointed person) registers under the simplified scheme and pays; for registered business recipients, ordinary reverse charge applies instead. The 2023 amendments deleted the minimal-human-intervention escape arguments by tightening the definition.

Registered persons with aggregate annual turnover above five crore rupees (in any year from 2017-18) must report B2B invoices to the Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an IRN and QR code — without which the invoice is not a valid invoice at all. B2C supplies, and notified exclusions like banks, insurers, GTAs and passenger transporters, stay outside. The e-invoice auto-populates GSTR-1 and travels with the e-way bill system.

Advance authorisation imports inputs duty-free for physical incorporation in export products, on actual user condition — the inputs and the resulting goods cannot be sold domestically until the export obligation is discharged. The scheme demands minimum value addition (generally fifteen per cent) and export within the specified period, with inputs quantified by standard input-output norms or self-declaration. It frees inputs; EPCG frees capital goods — parallel schemes, different subject matter.

concepts.subsection: Goods transport agencies — the two routes
concepts.statement: A GTA's services are taxed one of two ways: reverse charge at five per cent paid by the specified recipient with the GTA taking no input credit, or forward charge by the GTA's own annual declared option — at five per cent without credit or twelve per cent with full credit. Services to unregistered persons largely ride exemptions. The declaration binds for the financial year; recipients must know which regime their transporter elected, since the liability moves with it.

concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: An audit conducted under the Standards on Auditing obtains reasonable assurance, which is a high level of assurance but not absolute assurance.

concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: The audit is planned and performed with professional skepticism — a questioning mind alert to conditions indicating possible misstatement, and a critical assessment of evidence. It neither assumes management dishonest nor assumes it honest; records are accepted as genuine absent reason to believe otherwise, and doubted the moment there is one.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: The preconditions for an audit are an acceptable financial reporting framework and management's agreement to the premise on which an audit is conducted — its responsibility for the financial statements, for internal control, and for giving the auditor access and information. Where the preconditions are not present, the auditor does not accept the engagement.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: Where management imposes a limitation on scope before the engagement is accepted, and the auditor expects that limitation will result in a disclaimer of opinion, the auditor does not accept the engagement unless law or regulation requires it.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: On recurring audits the auditor assesses whether circumstances require the engagement terms to be revised and whether the entity needs reminding of the existing terms. A fresh letter every year is not demanded; a changed situation — new management, changed ownership, a changed framework, misunderstood scope — is what calls for one.

concepts.subsection: SA 220 (Revised) — Quality Management for an Audit
concepts.statement: The engagement partner takes overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the engagement. Work may be delegated across the engagement team, but the responsibility for quality is not delegated with it.
The final audit file is assembled ordinarily within not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report.

Audit documentation must be sufficient for an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the audit to understand the procedures performed, the results and evidence obtained, and the significant matters and conclusions. The file must speak for itself; the auditor's memory is not part of the record.

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: Management override of controls is a significant risk presumed to be present in every audit, and it is not rebuttable.

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: There is a presumed risk of fraud in revenue recognition, and unlike management override that presumption may be rebutted with documented reasons.

concepts.subsection: Auditor resignation under the Companies Act
concepts.statement: An auditor who resigns files a statement in the prescribed form with the company and the Registrar within thirty days of resignation, stating the reasons and any relevant facts. For specified companies the statement also goes to the Comptroller and Auditor-General. Failure invites a penalty on the auditor personally.

concepts.subsection: SA 250 — Consideration of Laws and Regulations
concepts.statement: SA 250 splits laws into two categories, and the auditor's responsibility differs between them. For laws with a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about compliance. For other laws that are fundamental to the operating aspects of the business, the auditor only performs specified procedures to help identify non-compliance.

concepts.subsection: SA 260 (Revised) — Communication with Those Charged with Governance
concepts.statement: The auditor communicates the planned scope and timing of the audit to those charged with governance, not only the findings.

concepts.subsection: SA 265 — Communicating Deficiencies in Internal Control
concepts.statement: Significant deficiencies in internal control are communicated in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis.

concepts.subsection: SA 299 (Revised) — Joint Audit of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Each joint auditor is responsible for the work divided to that auditor, and all joint auditors are jointly and severally responsible for the work not divided.

concepts.subsection: SA 315 (Revised) — Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement
concepts.statement: A significant risk is one requiring special audit consideration, and for such risks the auditor must obtain an understanding of the entity's related controls.

concepts.subsection: SA 320 — Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit
concepts.statement: Performance materiality is set below materiality for the financial statements as a whole, to reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements aggregate above materiality.

concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: When the auditor has determined that an assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level is a significant risk, substantive procedures specifically responsive to that risk must be performed.

concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: Irrespective of the assessed risks, the auditor designs and performs substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, account balance and disclosure. Excellent controls reduce substantive work; they never reduce it to zero for anything material.

concepts.subsection: SA 402 — Audit Considerations Relating to an Entity Using a Service Organisation
concepts.statement: A Type 1 report describes the service organisation's system and the design of its controls at a point in time. A Type 2 report also reports on their operating effectiveness over a period. Only a Type 2 report can give evidence about operating effectiveness.

concepts.subsection: SA 450 — Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
concepts.statement: Uncorrected misstatements are communicated to those charged with governance and the auditor evaluates whether they are material individually or in aggregate.
Sufficiency is the measure of the quantity of audit evidence; appropriateness is the measure of its quality, being its relevance and its reliability.

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Specific Considerations for Selected Items
concepts.statement: When inventory is material to the financial statements, the auditor must attend the physical inventory counting unless it is impracticable.

Where inventory held by a third party is material, the auditor obtains evidence of its existence and condition by requesting confirmation from the custodian, or by inspection, or both — and considers whether more is needed where the custodian's integrity or independence is in doubt.

Negative confirmations may be used as the sole substantive procedure only when the assessed risk is low, the population is large and homogeneous, a very low exception rate is expected, and the auditor is not aware of circumstances that would cause recipients to disregard them.

concepts.subsection: SA 510 — Initial Audit Engagements: Opening Balances
concepts.statement: In an initial audit engagement the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements, and whether accounting policies reflected in the opening balances have been consistently applied.

Analytical procedures are mandatory at two points in an audit — as risk assessment procedures during planning, and near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion. Using them as substantive procedures is optional, a choice the auditor makes about how to respond to an assessed risk.

Misstatements found in a sample are projected to the population the sample was drawn from. The sample is a means of reaching a conclusion about the whole population, so the error found in it is evidence about the whole population, not only about the items examined.

The auditor reviews the outcome, or subsequent re-estimation, of the prior period's accounting estimates — not to second-guess last year's audit, but to learn how management estimates: where its judgments proved biased, where uncertainty was understated, and where this year's risk therefore sits. Estimates resolved far from their booked amounts are risk assessment gold, not automatic prior-period errors.

A significant related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business gives rise to a significant risk. The auditor inspects the underlying contracts and evaluates whether the business rationale suggests the transaction was entered into to engage in fraudulent financial reporting or to conceal misappropriation of assets.
Where the report is amended for a subsequent event, dual dating confines the auditor's responsibility for events after the original date to that amendment alone.

Between the financial statements' date and the auditor's report date, the auditor actively performs procedures to catch events needing adjustment or disclosure. After the report's date the duty to search ends — but a fact coming to the auditor's knowledge before the statements are issued, which would have changed the report, must be pursued: discuss, determine amendment, and act on the outcome.

Where a material uncertainty about going concern exists and is adequately disclosed, the opinion is unmodified and a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" is included.

Written representations are audit evidence, but they are not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters they deal with. Obtaining them does not affect the nature or extent of the other evidence the auditor obtains.

concepts.subsection: SA 600 — Using the Work of Another Auditor
concepts.statement: Where a principal auditor uses the work of another auditor for a component, the principal auditor states the division of responsibility in the audit report, indicating the extent of the financial information audited by the other auditor. The principal auditor is not responsible for the work entrusted to the other auditor, except where circumstances should have aroused suspicion about its reliability.

concepts.subsection: SA 610 (Revised) — Using the Work of Internal Auditors
concepts.statement: SA 610 (Revised) permits internal auditors to provide direct assistance under the external auditor's direction, supervision and review — but never for procedures that involve significant judgments, relate to higher assessed risks where more than limited judgment is required, or cover work the internal audit function has itself reported on. Written agreements from the entity and the internal auditors come first.

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — Using the Work of an Auditor's Expert
concepts.statement: The auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion, and that responsibility is not reduced by using the work of an auditor's expert. The auditor's report does not refer to the expert unless the reference is required by law or regulation, and where it is, the report must state that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility.

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — Forming an Opinion and Reporting
concepts.statement: The auditor's report presents the Opinion as its first section, and the Basis for Opinion comes directly after it. The conclusion is stated before the reasons for it, so a reader who stops after the first paragraph has still read the opinion.
Key audit matters are required for audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, and where otherwise required by law or voluntarily undertaken.
A material misstatement that is not pervasive gives a qualified opinion; a material misstatement that is pervasive gives an adverse opinion.

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements; an Other Matter paragraph refers to a matter not so disclosed but relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report.

concepts.subsection: SA 710 — Comparative Information: Corresponding Figures and Comparative Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Where comparatives are presented as corresponding figures, the auditor's opinion refers to the current period only and does not refer to the corresponding figures. Where they are presented as comparative financial statements, the opinion refers to each period for which financial statements are presented.

concepts.subsection: SA 720 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Other Information
concepts.statement: The auditor reads the other information in the annual report and considers whether it is materially inconsistent with the financial statements or with the auditor's knowledge obtained in the audit. The auditor does not audit the other information and expresses no opinion or conclusion on it.

concepts.subsection: SA 800 — Special Considerations, Special Purpose Frameworks
concepts.statement: Financial statements prepared for specific users under a special purpose framework — a tax basis, a regulator's format, a contract's accounting clauses — are audited with the SAs applied to that framework, and the report carries an Emphasis of Matter alerting readers that the statements follow a special purpose framework and may be unsuitable for any other purpose; the auditor may also restrict distribution. The opinion itself is not modified by the framework being special.

citation.ref: special purpose framework reporting — Emphasis of Matter alert

items.stem: What is the company's WACC for discounting project cash flows?

options.text: 12.0 per cent, using the book-value weights of 625:375 with the after-tax cost of debt
options.misconception: weights the sources of capital by book value instead of the market value the firm actually raises money at
options.why: The book split is 500:300, or weights of 0.625 and 0.375. Applying those to 15% and 7% gives 9.375% + 2.625% = 12.0% — the after-tax cost of debt is right here, but market value, not book value, is what WACC must weight.

options.text: 14.0 per cent, using market-value weights but the pre-tax cost of debt of 10 per cent
options.misconception: omits the tax shield on interest, using debt's quoted rate instead of its after-tax cost
options.why: Interest is tax-deductible, so debt's true cost to the firm is 10% × (1 − 0.3) = 7%, not 10%. Using the pre-tax figure gives 0.8 × 15% + 0.2 × 10% = 14.0%, overstating the discount rate.

options.text: 13.4 per cent, using market-value weights of 80:20 and an after-tax cost of debt of 7 per cent
options.why: Weights come from market value: 800/1000 = 0.8 for equity, 200/1000 = 0.2 for debt. Debt's after-tax cost is 10% × (1 − 0.3) = 7%. WACC = 0.8 × 15% + 0.2 × 7% = 12% + 1.4% = 13.4%.

options.text: 8.6 per cent, using the market-value weights but assigning equity's weight to debt and debt's weight to equity
options.misconception: swaps the equity and debt weights before applying them to their respective costs
options.why: Swapping the weights gives 0.2 × 15% + 0.8 × 7% = 3% + 5.6% = 8.6%, understating WACC by crediting the cheaper source with the larger share it does not actually have.

items.scenario: A company's equity has a market value of ₹800 crore and a cost of equity of 15 per cent. Its debt has a market value of ₹200 crore and a pre-tax cost of 10 per cent. The tax rate is 30 per cent. The same company's books show equity at ₹500 crore and debt at ₹300 crore.

items.stem: Under real options reasoning, what should the firm do and why?

options.text: Reject — total value is −5 − 9 = −₹14 crore, since the option adds another cost on top of the shortfall
options.misconception: subtracts the option value instead of adding it, treating flexibility as a further cost rather than a source of value
options.why: An option the firm holds, not one it owes, only ever adds to value — it is the right, not the obligation, to expand. It is added to static NPV, giving +4 crore, not subtracted.

options.text: Reject — the static NPV is −5 crore and real options do not change accept-or-reject decisions
options.misconception: treats real options as inapplicable and evaluates the project on static NPV alone
options.why: The whole point of real options is that flexibility has value discounting misses. A project rejected on static NPV alone can still be strategically positive once its embedded options are priced in, as here.

options.text: Accept — total strategic value is −5 + 9 = ₹4 crore, since the expansion option is worth more than the pilot's shortfall
options.why: Real options add the option's value to the static NPV rather than ignoring it: −5 + 9 = +4 crore. Discounting alone prices the pilot as if the expansion choice did not exist, which is exactly what real options corrects.

options.text: Accept, with total value of ₹9 crore, since only the option matters once one exists
options.misconception: credits the option value alone and drops the underlying project's own negative static NPV
options.why: The option sits on top of the base project, not instead of it. Both figures belong in the total: −5 crore from the pilot itself, +9 crore from the option to expand, netting to +4 crore.

items.scenario: A pilot plant has a static NPV of −₹5 crore on its own cash flows. It also carries the option to expand into a full plant in three years if the pilot succeeds; that option, valued separately, is worth ₹9 crore.

items.stem: Which technique is this, and what does it give that changing one variable at a time cannot?

options.text: Scenario analysis — because it uses a set of named cases such as best, base and worst
options.misconception: mistakes the description of scenario analysis's few discrete bundles for a method that draws thousands of random combinations
options.why: Scenario analysis bundles a handful of internally consistent cases by name. Ten thousand random draws from each variable's own distribution is a different exercise entirely — simulation, not a short list of scenarios.

options.text: Sensitivity analysis — because several variables are varied at the same time
options.misconception: defines sensitivity analysis by the number of variables moved, when its defining trait is moving exactly one at a time
options.why: Sensitivity analysis isolates one variable, holding the rest fixed, precisely so each variable's own break-even point is visible. Moving several together, randomly, is what simulation does.

options.text: Simulation — a full probability distribution of NPV, including the chance of a negative outcome, not just a handful of break-even points
options.why: Drawing many random combinations from probability distributions and building the full outcome spread is Monte Carlo simulation. Sensitivity analysis only ever answers "what if this one variable moves," never the chance of any particular result.

options.text: The certainty equivalent approach — because it converts risky flows into a single risk-adjusted figure
options.misconception: confuses simulation's output, a distribution of outcomes, with the certainty equivalent method's output, a single deflated cash flow
options.why: Certainty equivalents shrink each risky flow to one certain-equivalent number and discount it at the risk-free rate. That produces one adjusted NPV, not the spread of ten thousand outcomes described here.

items.scenario: An analyst reruns a project's NPV model ten thousand times, each run drawing sales volume, selling price and unit cost independently from their own probability distributions, and plots the resulting spread of ten thousand NPV outcomes.

items.stem: What is the one-step binomial value of the call?

options.text: ₹12.00, the expected payoff at the correct risk-neutral probability, left undiscounted
options.misconception: computes the correct expected payoff but forgets to discount it back to the present at the risk-free rate
options.why: 0.6 × 20 = ₹12 is the expected payoff one period from now, not its value today. The option's price is that payoff discounted at 1.08, giving ₹11.11, not ₹12.00.

options.text: ₹9.26, taking the up and down moves as equally likely instead of computing the risk-neutral probability
options.misconception: substitutes a naive 50-50 probability for the no-arbitrage risk-neutral probability the model requires
options.why: At p = 0.5 the expected payoff would be 0.5 × 20 = ₹10, discounting to 10/1.08 ≈ ₹9.26. But 0.5 is not the probability that removes arbitrage here — 0.6 is, from the risk-free rate and the up and down factors.

options.text: ₹11.11: risk-neutral probability 0.6, expected payoff ₹12, discounted at 1.08
options.why: p = (1.08 − 0.9) / (1.2 − 0.9) = 0.18/0.3 = 0.6, using u = 1.2 and d = 0.9. Payoffs are ₹20 up and ₹0 down, so expected payoff = 0.6 × 20 = ₹12, discounted at 1.08 gives 12/1.08 ≈ ₹11.11.

options.text: ₹7.41, swapping u and d in the risk-neutral probability formula
options.misconception: swaps the up and down factors inside the probability formula, inverting which state is which
options.why: Swapping gives p = (1.08 − 1.2)/(0.9 − 1.2) = 0.4, not 0.6. Expected payoff falls to 0.4 × 20 = ₹8, discounting to 8/1.08 ≈ ₹7.41 — a probability drawn from the wrong pairing of factor to state.

items.scenario: A share trading at ₹100 will move in one period to either ₹120 or ₹90. The risk-free growth factor for the period is 1.08. A call option on the share has a strike of ₹100.

items.stem: What happens to the two premiums?

options.text: The call rises and the put falls by the same amount, to keep put-call parity satisfied
options.misconception: misapplies put-call parity, which fixes call-minus-put, to mean the two must move in opposite directions
options.why: Parity fixes C − P at a value independent of volatility, which both premiums rising together, by the same amount, still satisfies exactly. Parity requires them to move together, not apart.

options.text: Only the call premium rises, since higher volatility only helps a bet on the price going up
options.misconception: assumes volatility only benefits upside bets, when a put profits just as much from a large favourable (downward) move
options.why: A put gains from a big fall the same way a call gains from a big rise; both are bets on movement, not direction. Volatility raises the value of optionality on both sides at once.

options.text: Both premiums fall, since higher volatility is priced as a risk cost the way it would depress a bond's price
options.misconception: treats volatility like a bond's default or duration risk, which lowers value, instead of like optionality, which volatility raises
options.why: Unlike a bond holder, an option holder's downside is fixed at the premium already paid while the upside is open-ended, so more volatility can only help, never hurt, the option's value.

options.text: Both the call and the put premium rise
options.why: Higher volatility raises the chance of a large favourable move for either option, while the loss on each stays capped at its premium — so both gain value together, and by the same amount, since put-call parity's right-hand side does not depend on volatility.

items.scenario: A dealer revises only her volatility estimate for an underlying share upward, holding spot, strike, time to expiry and the risk-free rate unchanged, and reprices both a call and a put on that share with Black-Scholes.

items.stem: What price does the convexity-adjusted estimate give, and how does it compare with the duration-only estimate?

options.text: ₹880 — the duration-only fall of 12 per cent, with convexity ignored entirely
options.misconception: uses the linear duration estimate alone and skips the convexity correction altogether
options.why: −6 × 0.02 = −12% gives ₹880, but that straight-line estimate overstates the loss for a positive-convexity bond — the true fall is smaller once the 1.6% convexity add-back is included.

options.text: ₹896 — a 10.4 per cent fall, softer than the 12 per cent duration-only fall because convexity adds back 1.6 per cent
options.why: Duration-only: −6 × 0.02 = −12%. Convexity term: 0.5 × 80 × 0.02² = 0.5 × 80 × 0.0004 = 1.6%. Combined: −12% + 1.6% = −10.4%, so price = 1,000 × 0.896 = ₹896 — less severe than the straight-line estimate, as positive convexity always is on a yield rise.

options.text: ₹912 — omitting the one-half factor in the convexity term
options.misconception: drops the standard one-half multiplier on the convexity term, overstating the correction
options.why: The convexity adjustment is 0.5 × C × (Δy)², not C × (Δy)²  — the one-half comes from the second-derivative term in the Taylor expansion the estimate is built on. Skipping it gives 3.2% instead of 1.6%, and an overstated ₹912.

options.text: ₹864 — subtracting the convexity term from the duration estimate instead of adding it
options.misconception: subtracts the convexity term from the duration-only estimate, doubling the mis-estimate of the loss instead of correcting it
options.why: The convexity term is always added, not subtracted: −12% + 1.6% = −10.4%, not −12% − 1.6% = −13.6%. Positive convexity works in the bondholder's favour on both a rise and a fall in yield, so it can only soften a loss, never worsen it.

items.scenario: A bond priced at ₹1,000 has a modified duration of 6 years and a convexity of 80. Its yield rises by 200 basis points.

items.stem: What is the bond's current yield, and how does it sit against the coupon rate and the yield to maturity?

options.text: 8.33 per cent, dividing the coupon by the average of price and face value
options.misconception: applies the approximate-YTM shortcut, which averages price and face value in its denominator, to a plain current-yield question
options.why: Current yield only ever divides by the market price: 80/920 ≈ 8.70%. Averaging price and face value, 80/960 ≈ 8.33%, belongs to an approximation of YTM, a different figure answering a different question.

options.text: 8.70 per cent — above the 8.00 per cent coupon, with YTM higher again, since a discount bond also gains from the pull to par
options.why: Current yield = 80/920 ≈ 8.70%, above the 8.00% coupon because the price sits below face value. YTM adds the capital gain to par at redemption on top of that, so the order is coupon rate < current yield < YTM for any discount bond.

options.text: 8.70 per cent, but with YTM the lowest of the three since the discounted price marks the bond as cheap
options.misconception: reverses the ordering, reading a discount price as depressing the yield instead of raising it further still through the pull to par
options.why: A price below par is exactly what makes YTM the highest of the three, not the lowest — the buyer collects both the coupon stream and the gain to par at maturity. The current yield figure of 8.70% is right; the ordering claimed after it is not.

options.text: 8.00 per cent, dividing the coupon by the face value rather than the market price
options.misconception: computes current yield on face value instead of the bond's actual market price
options.why: Current yield is defined against what the bond actually costs today, ₹920, not its ₹1,000 face value. 80/1,000 = 8.00% is just the coupon rate restated, not the yield an investor buying at ₹920 earns.

items.scenario: An 8 per cent coupon bond with face value ₹1,000 is trading at ₹920.

items.stem: Ignoring time value of money, what is the bank's net cash flow across the premiums paid and the default payout?

options.text: Net gain of ₹6 crore, the payout alone, with the premiums paid left out of the reckoning
options.misconception: reports the default payout as the net benefit and forgets to deduct the premiums paid over the life of the position
options.why: The premiums are a real cost the buyer paid every year the contract ran, ₹0.45 crore in total here, and belong in the net figure alongside the ₹6 crore payout: 6 − 0.45 = ₹5.55 crore.

options.text: Net gain of ₹9.55 crore, with the payout set at the full ₹10 crore face value
options.misconception: pays out the full face value instead of the loss given default, ignoring the stated 40 per cent recovery rate
options.why: The seller's obligation is the loss given default, ₹10 crore × (1 − 0.4) = ₹6 crore, not the whole face value. Paying the full ₹10 crore ignores the recovery the bond still returns.

options.text: Net gain of ₹5.55 crore — a ₹6 crore payout on the 60 per cent loss given default, less ₹0.45 crore of premiums paid over three years
options.why: Premiums: ₹10 crore × 1.5% × 3 years = ₹0.45 crore. Payout: (1 − 0.4) × ₹10 crore = ₹6 crore, since the seller covers only the loss given default, not the whole face value. Net: 6 − 0.45 = ₹5.55 crore.

options.text: Net gain of ₹5.25 crore, continuing to count premiums for the full five-year tenor even though default ended the contract in year 3
options.misconception: keeps paying CDS premiums out to the original five-year tenor instead of stopping at the default that ends the contract
options.why: Protection ends when the reference entity defaults; only the premiums actually paid up to that point, two years' worth here, count. Charging five years of premium against a contract that ended in year 3 overstates the cost and understates the net gain.

items.scenario: A bank holds a ₹10 crore bond and buys five-year CDS protection on it at a spread of 150 basis points a year, paid annually. The reference entity defaults at the start of year 3, after two full annual premiums have been paid, and the recovery rate is 40 per cent.

items.stem: What is the theoretical ex-rights price, and what is the value of the right attached to one existing share?

options.text: TERP ₹130; value of the right ₹5 per existing share, taking a simple average of the cum-rights and issue prices
options.misconception: averages the cum-rights and subscription prices equally instead of weighting them by the number of shares outstanding at each price
options.why: A simple average, (150 + 110)/2 = ₹130, ignores that four times as many shares trade at ₹150 as are issued at ₹110. The weighted figure, ₹142, reflects that four-to-one mix; a plain average does not.

options.text: TERP unchanged at ₹150; value of the right ₹40, the gap between the cum-rights price and the subscription price
options.misconception: ignores the dilution the new shares cause, comparing the subscription price to the undiluted cum-rights price instead of the ex-rights price
options.why: Once the new shares are issued, the price settles at the blended ex-rights figure, ₹142, not the pre-issue ₹150. The right's value is 142 − 110 = ₹32, spread over four shares — ₹150 − 110 = ₹40 skips the dilution the rights issue itself causes.

options.text: TERP ₹142; value of the right ₹8 per existing share
options.why: TERP = (4cr × 150 + 1cr × 110) / 5cr = (600 + 110)/5 = ₹142. The right to buy one new share is worth 142 − 110 = ₹32; spread over the four old shares needed to earn it, that is ₹8 per existing share.

options.text: TERP ₹142; value of the right ₹6.40 per existing share, dividing by the post-issue share count of five instead of four
options.misconception: divides the right's value by the total post-issue share count instead of the subscription ratio of old shares needed for one new share
options.why: The right's ₹32 value belongs to the four old shares that earn one new share under a 1-for-4 issue, so 32/4 = ₹8. Dividing by five, the post-issue total, answers a different question and understates the figure.

items.scenario: A company with 4 crore shares outstanding, trading cum-rights at ₹150, offers a 1-for-4 rights issue — one new share for every four held — at a subscription price of ₹110.

items.stem: What does Walter's model give as the share price at this payout, and what does it say the firm should do?

options.text: About ₹73.33, inverting the ratio to Ke/r instead of r/Ke
options.misconception: inverts the r/Ke multiplier in Walter's formula, understating what retained earnings contribute for a growth firm
options.why: Using Ke/r = 0.12/0.15 = 0.8 gives [4 + 0.8 × 6]/0.12 = 8.8/0.12 ≈ ₹73.33. The formula's multiplier is r/Ke = 1.25, which rewards a firm earning above its cost of equity — the inverted ratio does the opposite.

options.text: About ₹95.83; since r (15%) exceeds Ke (12%), the firm should retain more and cut its payout further to raise the price above this
options.why: P = [4 + (0.15/0.12)(10 − 4)]/0.12 = [4 + 1.25 × 6]/0.12 = 11.5/0.12 ≈ ₹95.83. Because the firm earns more on retained cash than shareholders' own opportunity cost, Walter's rule says push retention toward 100%, not hold it at 40%.

options.text: About ₹95.83, but since r exceeds Ke the firm should raise its payout toward 100 per cent to maximise price
options.misconception: reverses Walter's decision rule, recommending higher payout for a growth firm when full retention is what maximises price
options.why: The price figure is right, but the direction is backwards. When r > Ke the firm compounds shareholders' money better than the market does, so the rule calls for retaining more, not distributing more.

options.text: ₹11.50, stopping at the formula's numerator and forgetting the final division by Ke
options.misconception: computes the numerator of Walter's formula correctly but omits the final division by the cost of equity
options.why: 4 + 1.25 × 6 = 11.5 is only the bracketed numerator; Walter's price is that figure divided by Ke, 11.5/0.12 ≈ ₹95.83, not the undiscounted 11.5 itself.

items.scenario: A company has EPS of ₹10, pays a dividend of ₹4 per share, earns an internal return of 15 per cent on retained earnings, and has a cost of equity of 12 per cent.

items.stem: What money multiple (MOIC) does the sponsor earn on exit, and what drove it?

options.text: 2.5x — exit equity of 500 − 250 = ₹250 crore against ₹100 crore of sponsor equity, driven purely by debt paydown
options.why: Exit equity value is enterprise value less the debt still outstanding: 500 − 250 = ₹250 crore. Against the ₹100 crore the sponsor put in, that is a 2.5x return, and since EBITDA and the multiple never moved, debt paydown alone explains it.

options.text: 1.5x — treating the ₹150 crore of debt paid down as if it were itself the exit equity value
options.misconception: equates the amount of debt paid down with the exit equity value, instead of computing exit enterprise value less remaining debt
options.why: Debt paid down (400 − 250 = 150) measures how much less is owed, not what the equity is worth. Equity value is what is left after debt: 500 − 250 = ₹250 crore, not the ₹150 crore paydown itself.

options.text: 5.0x — treating the full ₹500 crore exit enterprise value as belonging to the sponsor, with no debt netted off
options.misconception: forgets that debt still outstanding at exit belongs to the lenders, not the sponsor, and credits the whole enterprise value to equity
options.why: ₹250 crore of debt is still owed at exit and comes off the top before anything belongs to the sponsor. 500/100 = 5.0x skips that deduction entirely.

options.text: 1.0x — measuring the return on the unchanged ₹500 crore enterprise value rather than on the sponsor's equity slice
options.misconception: measures the return on the whole, unchanged enterprise value instead of the sponsor's leveraged equity slice, which is where the paydown accrues
