options.text: No, because digital services can never have an Indian business connection
options.misconception: right answer, mistaken ground
options.why: Domestically, SEP creates exactly that business connection — thresholds crossed, the hook holds. What saves the platform is the treaty override, not any gap in section 9.

options.text: Yes, because streaming into India constitutes a virtual permanent establishment
options.misconception: invents a PE category the treaty does not contain
options.why: PE under the treaty means fixed places, dependent agents and the like. Virtual presence concepts live in domestic law and multilateral proposals, not in the operative treaty text.

options.text: No — the treaty's permanent establishment article governs a treaty resident, and SEP cannot override it
options.why: Section 90(2) lets the taxpayer take the treaty where more beneficial, and the treaty taxes business profits only through a permanent establishment — which needs more than users and revenue. SEP rewrote the domestic definition of business connection, not the treaty; its practical reach is non-treaty jurisdictions, and this platform is not one.

options.text: Yes — SEP was enacted precisely to tax digital businesses like this one
options.misconception: reads the purpose while skipping the treaty ceiling
options.why: The purpose is real and the domestic hook now exists — but a treaty resident claims the treaty, and business profits without a PE stay untaxed here until the treaty itself changes.

items.scenario: A US-based streaming platform with no office, server or staff in India earns large subscription revenue from Indian users, crossing the significant economic presence thresholds. The platform is entitled to the India-US tax treaty. The assessing officer taxes its profits, holding that the SEP amendment overrides treaties as later domestic law.

items.stem: What can the trust actually do about the ₹25 lakh shortfall?

options.text: Carry it forward as next year's application, netting against next year's 85 per cent
options.misconception: invents inter-year set-off in the wrong direction
options.why: The regime tests each year's application against each year's income. The route forward for this year's surplus is 11(2) accumulation, not a credit against a future year's obligation.

options.text: Nothing — unspent income above fifteen per cent is taxable, full stop
options.misconception: reads section 11(1) without 11(2)
options.why: The five-year accumulation exists precisely for lumpy charitable projects like building wings. The accountant's rule is the default, not the last word.

options.text: Simply resolve to spend it eventually — charitable intention protects charitable money
options.misconception: substitutes intention for the statutory conditions
options.why: The shelter is procedural on purpose: stated purpose, filed statement, specified investments, five years. An unminuted intention satisfies none of them and the exemption fails.

options.text: Accumulate it for the hospital wing under section 11(2) — a specific purpose, the prescribed statement, and a five-year clock
options.why: Eighty-five per cent of ₹1 crore is ₹85 lakh; ₹60 lakh is applied and ₹15 lakh rides the standing accumulation, leaving ₹25 lakh exposed. Section 11(2) shelters it: name the specific purpose, file the statement before the return's due date, invest in specified modes, and spend within five years. Miss those conditions and the amount falls back into tax.

items.scenario: A registered charitable trust earns ₹1 crore in the year and spends ₹60 lakh on its school by 31 March. The trustees plan a hospital wing and want to keep the remaining ₹40 lakh for it, without tax. The accountant says the shortfall below eighty-five per cent is simply taxable and nothing can be done after the year has run.

items.stem: What is the correct capital gain?

options.text: ₹60 crore long-term — FMV of ₹130 crore as deemed consideration, less ₹70 crore net worth ignoring the revaluation
options.why: Two corrections: since the 2021 amendment, consideration is the higher rule-computed fair market value, ₹130 crore, not the ₹120 crore price; and net worth expressly ignores revaluation, so cost is ₹70 crore. Fifteen years of holding makes the gain long-term — the undertaking's age governs, depreciable contents notwithstanding.

options.text: Itemised gains asset by asset, since a lump sum must be allocated to compute anything
options.misconception: dissolves the slump sale into the piecemeal sale it is defined against
options.why: The absence of item-wise values is the definition of a slump sale, and section 50B exists to tax exactly that. Allocation would recreate the valuation disputes the lump-sum route avoids.

options.text: ₹60 crore, but short-term — the plant inside was depreciated, and depreciable assets always yield short-term gains
options.misconception: applies section 50's asset-level rule to an undertaking-level transfer
options.why: A slump sale taxes one capital asset — the undertaking. Its holding period, past thirty-six months, sets the character; the deeming for depreciable assets stays with itemised transfers.

options.text: ₹25 crore — price received less book net worth as stated
options.misconception: accepts both the stale consideration and the revalued cost
options.why: Each error flatters the taxpayer: revaluation inflates cost by ₹25 crore and the FMV deeming lifts consideration by ₹10 crore. The section blocks both doors by its terms.

items.scenario: A company sells its fifteen-year-old bottling division as a going concern for ₹120 crore lump sum. The division's net worth per the prescribed computation is ₹70 crore; its books show ₹95 crore after a recent upward revaluation of land. Rule-based fair market value of the undertaking is ₹130 crore. The CFO computes long-term gain of ₹25 crore (120 − 95).

items.stem: Is the tax team right?

options.text: Yes — TDS provisions apply only where money is paid or credited
options.misconception: states the pre-2022 gap the section was written to close
options.why: That reasoning is why dealer incentives escaped for years. Section 194R's words cover any benefit or perquisite, in cash or in kind or partly both.

options.text: No TDS, but each distributor must self-declare the trip's value in the return
options.misconception: relies on the recipient honesty the section stopped relying on
options.why: The benefit is taxable in the distributor's hands with or without 194R; the section exists because self-declaration of free trips was rare. The collection duty now sits with the provider.

options.text: No — section 194R reaches benefits in kind, and the company must ensure tax on ₹3 lakh per distributor is paid before the trip
options.why: The section was enacted for exactly this: benefits arising from business relationships that never touch a bank account. Each trip crosses the twenty-thousand threshold fifteen times over, and for a benefit wholly in kind the provider's duty is to ensure the tax is deposited — by collecting it from the distributor or bearing it grossed up — before release.

options.text: TDS applies, but on the company's cost of the trip after group discounts, at 2 per cent
options.misconception: right obligation, invented rate
options.why: The rate is ten per cent of the benefit's value. Valuation questions are real at the margin, but a fifth of the correct rate is not a valuation position.

items.scenario: A pharma company sends its top thirty distributors on a fully paid foreign conference trip worth ₹3 lakh each. No cash changes hands — the company books the travel directly. Its tax team sees no TDS obligation: nothing was paid to the distributors, and TDS attaches to payments.

items.stem: What does section 35 actually allow this year?

options.text: ₹2 crore only — capital expenditure must travel through depreciation
options.misconception: denies the section's central acceleration
options.why: Full-year deduction of capital research spend is precisely what distinguishes section 35 from ordinary depreciation. The equipment deducts now, once, entirely.

options.text: ₹7 crore — revenue and capital research expenditure in full, but nothing for the land
options.why: The salaries and materials deduct as revenue research expenditure, and the equipment deducts fully in the year despite being capital — that acceleration is the section's gift. Land is its stated exception: however research-bound, it neither deducts under 35 nor depreciates. The weighted era is over; one hundred per cent is the ceiling.

options.text: ₹10.5 crore — the 150 per cent weighting applies to the revenue portion
options.misconception: claims a sunset benefit
options.why: The weighted deductions were legislated down to one hundred per cent. Nostalgia for 150 per cent is now an excess claim inviting disallowance and penalty.

options.text: ₹10 crore — everything spent in the direction of research qualifies
options.misconception: reads the capital allowance without its land exception
options.why: The section says expenditure of a capital nature excluding land. Land appreciates and waits; Parliament declined to fund patience.

items.scenario: A manufacturing company spends during the year on in-house research related to its business: ₹2 crore on scientists' salaries and materials, ₹5 crore on laboratory equipment, and ₹3 crore on land beside the factory for a future research block. The CFO claims ₹10 crore under section 35, recalling that research once earned a weighted 150 per cent, and hoping at least 100 per cent survives for all of it.

items.stem: Where is the company's POEM?

options.text: In India, but only its Indian-sourced income becomes taxable
options.misconception: gives residence the consequences of source
options.why: Residence brings worldwide income within reach, subject to treaty relief. Source-only taxation is the regime the company just lost.

options.text: In Singapore — the board is the organ of management and it met there
options.misconception: reads the minutes as the management
options.why: Formal authority matters when actually exercised. POEM was adopted precisely to see through boards that convene abroad to bless decisions made at home.

options.text: Nowhere taxable — a subsidiary's decisions naturally involve its parent, which cannot create residence
options.misconception: stretches shareholder oversight into a safe harbour
options.why: Guidance distinguishes a parent's governance influence from the subsidiary's own decisions being taken by the parent's officers. Selecting this company's suppliers and prices is the latter.

options.text: In India — decisions are made in substance in Mumbai, and Singapore's minutes record ratification, not management
options.why: The test asks where key management and commercial decisions are in substance made. A board that rubber-stamps Mumbai's emails has moved the venue of signatures, not of management; the effective decisions travel with the CFO. The company is resident, and its global income enters the Indian net for the year.

items.scenario: A Singapore-incorporated trading subsidiary of an Indian group holds all board meetings in Singapore, minuted meticulously. The evidence shows every significant decision — supplier selection, pricing, financing — is made by the group CFO in Mumbai and emailed to the Singapore directors, who approve without discussion. The company claims non-resident status on the strength of its meeting venue.

items.stem: What can the Commissioner (Appeals) lawfully do?

options.text: Enhance by the ₹3 crore after a show-cause opportunity — but not remand; the appeal must be decided
options.why: Section 251 arms the first appellate authority with enhancement, so an appeal can leave the taxpayer worse off — counsel's floor does not exist, though the power runs only after a reasonable opportunity to show cause. The remand power was deliberately removed: the file's quality is the Commissioner's problem to cure by enquiry and decision, not to return to sender.

options.text: Enhance immediately — the taxpayer invited full scrutiny by appealing
options.misconception: skips the mandatory hearing
options.why: Enhancement without a show-cause opportunity fails the section's own condition and natural justice with it. The power is real; the process is not optional.

options.text: Neither — an appellate authority is confined to the grounds the taxpayer raised
options.misconception: shrinks the first appeal to the appellant's agenda
options.why: The first appeal is a re-look at the assessment, with the assessment's subject matter open. Enhancement on connected matters within it is the statute's express grant.

options.text: Both — appellate powers include everything the assessing officer could do
options.misconception: keeps the abolished remand alive
options.why: The set-aside-and-remand power was taken away by amendment. Deciding, with enquiry where needed, is now the only route through.

items.scenario: Appealing a ₹2 crore addition, a taxpayer's counsel is confident: at worst the addition stands. Reviewing the file, the Commissioner (Appeals) notices a related deduction the assessing officer allowed that looks untenable, worth another ₹3 crore, and also considers sending the whole case back for a fresh assessment given the file's poor quality.

items.stem: How is the December 2025 buy-back actually taxed for her?

options.text: Capital gains of ₹8 lakh — consideration less cost, like any share sale
options.misconception: taxes the buy-back as an ordinary transfer
options.why: The deeming intercepts the consideration and calls all of it dividend. The capital gains computation still runs, but with nil consideration — yielding a loss, not the ₹8 lakh gain.

options.text: Dividend of ₹8 lakh — the deeming nets off her cost first
options.misconception: imports a cost deduction the provision denies
options.why: The dividend is the entire sum received; cost has no place in dividend taxation. Its only outlet is the engineered capital loss on the side.

options.text: Exempt in her hands — the company discharges the buy-back tax under section 115QA
options.misconception: applies the pre-October 2024 regime
options.why: Section 115QA and the shareholder exemption ceased for buy-backs from 1 October 2024. Answering the old law on a December 2025 buy-back is the error this change was bound to produce.

options.text: The full ₹20 lakh is her dividend income at slab rates, and the ₹12 lakh cost becomes a capital loss usable only against capital gains
options.why: From 1 October 2024 the exemption and the company-level tax are both gone: the whole consideration is deemed dividend under section 2(22)(f), with TDS and slab taxation, and no cost deduction against it. The cost is preserved separately — consideration deemed nil produces a ₹12 lakh capital loss to set off or carry forward against capital gains alone, never against the dividend.

items.scenario: In December 2025 a listed company buys back shares at ₹1,000 each. An investor tenders 2,000 shares bought years ago at ₹600. Remembering the old regime, she expects the ₹20 lakh receipt to be exempt in her hands with the company paying the buy-back tax, and asks only whether her ₹12 lakh cost still matters.

items.stem: Does section 2(22)(e) bite?

options.text: No — the recipient is the firm, and dividends can only accrue to shareholders
options.misconception: reads the section without its concern limb
options.why: The concern limb exists because sole reliance on direct loans made avoidance trivial. The deemed dividend is assessed in the hands the provision names, detour notwithstanding.

options.text: No, because a repaid loan was never income in substance
options.misconception: lets subsequent events rewrite the taxable event
options.why: The mischief is shareholders enjoying company profits as untaxed loans. A rotating loan — drawn, repaid, redrawn — would otherwise deliver dividends perpetually tax free.

options.text: Yes, but only ₹2 crore times his 40 per cent shareholding
options.misconception: apportions a deeming that attaches to the payment
options.why: The deemed dividend is the payment itself, capped by accumulated profits — not a pro-rata slice of it. His shareholding qualifies the trigger; it does not dilute the amount.

options.text: Yes — a loan to a concern in which the substantial shareholder is substantially interested is deemed dividend, and repayment does not erase it
options.why: The provision expressly reaches payments to any concern in which such a shareholder holds substantial interest — routing through the firm is the oldest detour it closed. The deeming operates when the loan is made, to the extent of accumulated profits; repayment seven months later no more undoes it than returning a dividend would. Market interest helps commercial optics, not the statutory deeming.

items.scenario: A private company with ₹5 crore of accumulated profits lends ₹2 crore to a partnership firm in which its 40 per cent shareholder is a partner with a substantial interest. The loan carries market interest and is repaid in full within seven months. The shareholder argues no dividend can arise: the money went to the firm, not to him, and it came back.

items.stem: Is the set-off valid?

options.text: Yes, against the futures profit at least — both involve the stock market
options.misconception: matches by market instead of by statutory character
options.why: The futures profit is expressly non-speculative; the share loss is deemed speculative. Statutory characters, not trading venues, decide who may meet whom — and these two are on opposite sides.

options.text: Yes — delivery-based share trading is never speculation, so the loss is ordinary business loss
options.misconception: applies section 43(5) and skips the company-specific Explanation
options.why: For individuals that is the end of it. For companies the Explanation adds a deeming on top of the definition, and this company fits none of its exceptions.

options.text: No — the Explanation deems the company's share-trading loss speculative, and speculation loss cannot touch the distribution profit or even the F&O profit
options.why: Delivery normally saves a transaction from being speculative, but the Explanation to section 73 deems a company's share-dealing business speculation regardless of delivery, unless the company is in the carved-out classes. The loss can meet only speculation profit — and the index futures profit is statutorily not speculative, being eligible exchange-traded derivatives. The ₹50 lakh waits, four years at most, for a speculation profit that may never come.

options.text: No set-off ever — deemed speculation losses lapse the same year
options.misconception: denies the carry-forward the section grants
options.why: The loss survives four assessment years, usable against any speculation profit arising in them. Restrictive is not the same as extinguished.

items.scenario: A trading company (not an investment or banking company) has three results this year: ₹50 lakh loss from its business of buying and selling listed shares with delivery; ₹20 lakh profit from exchange-traded index futures; and ₹80 lakh profit from its commodities distribution business. It sets the share loss against the distribution profit.

items.stem: Who is right about the ₹8 lakh?

options.text: The colleague — aggregation means the whole ₹20 lakh bears tax
options.misconception: converts a rate device into a charge
options.why: Taxing farm income is beyond Parliament's chosen scheme — agriculture is the States' field. The two-step computation deducts the farm slice back out, leaving only the rate effect.

options.text: The scheme applies, but only if agricultural income exceeds the business income
options.misconception: invents a proportionality condition
options.why: The gates are five thousand rupees of farm income and other income above the basic exemption — both crossed here. Relative size is nowhere in the test.

options.text: The accountant — exempt means the ₹8 lakh never enters any computation
options.misconception: reads the exemption as invisibility
options.why: Total invisibility would let a large landowner's modest business income enjoy the lowest slabs. The rate integration exists to price ability to pay without taxing the exempt source.

options.text: Neither — the farm income is not taxed, but it fixes the rate: tax on ₹20 lakh, less tax on the agricultural income plus the exemption limit
options.why: Partial integration threads between the two errors. Aggregating ₹20 lakh pushes the business income into the slabs it would occupy if the taxpayer's true capacity were visible; the deduction of tax on agricultural income plus the exemption limit then returns what would have fallen on the farm income itself. The exemption holds; only the rate feels the farm.

citation.ref: Section 10(1) with Finance Act rate schedule

items.scenario: An individual under the old regime has business income of ₹12 lakh and net agricultural income of ₹8 lakh. His accountant computes tax on ₹12 lakh alone, citing the exemption of agricultural income; a colleague objects that the ₹8 lakh must be added and taxed like any other income.

items.stem: What does section 43B allow this year?

options.text: The GST and the interest — the bank's acceptance of the conversion discharged the liability
options.misconception: treats novation as payment
options.why: The liability was rearranged, not extinguished by outflow; not a rupee left the company. The Explanation names this arrangement and denies it.

options.text: All three — mercantile accounting deducts what accrues
options.misconception: reads the books where the section reads the bank statement
options.why: Section 43B exists to override accrual for exactly these sums, which taxpayers accrued for decades and paid never. The non obstante clause beats the method of accounting.

options.text: Only the GST — the late bonus waits for its payment year, and the conversion of interest into a loan is statutorily not payment
options.why: Payment by the due date of the return preserves accrual-year deduction, which saves the GST. The bonus missed that date, so it deducts in the year actually paid. The interest is the trap the Explanations closed in terms: conversion into a loan or borrowing is not actual payment, and the deduction arrives only as the converted loan is repaid.

options.text: The GST and the bonus — employee dues enjoy a grace period until actually paid
options.misconception: invents a bonus concession beyond the due-date proviso
options.why: The proviso's grace runs to the return's due date for every 43B sum alike. A March payment is eleven months past it; the deduction simply shifts years.

items.scenario: At year-end a company's books accrue: GST of ₹80 lakh, paid in full in May, well before the return's due date; bonus of ₹40 lakh, paid the following March, after the return was filed; and ₹1.2 crore of interest owed to its bank, which the bank agreed to convert into a fresh term loan in February. The company claims all three this year.

items.stem: What is the correct withholding position on these purchases?

options.text: Both deduct and collect, at 0.1 per cent each, as the sections literally overlap
options.misconception: revives the overlap the omission dissolved
options.why: Even in the overlap era the buyer's TDS took precedence and switched the TCS off. Now there is no second provision at all.

options.text: The buyer deducts 0.1 per cent on ₹1.4 crore — seller-side TCS on goods is gone, and the buyer's duty stands alone
options.why: Turnover above ten crore makes the manufacturer a specified buyer, and purchases beyond fifty lakh from one seller trigger deduction on the excess — ₹1.4 crore here, a modest ₹14,000 of tax but a serious obligation. The TCS the accountant is waiting for was omitted from 1 April 2025; nobody else is collecting, and the failure prices itself through the 30 per cent expense disallowance.

options.text: The seller collects TCS at 0.1 per cent, and the buyer rightly does nothing
options.misconception: relies on the omitted collection provision
options.why: That was the fallback half of an overlap that ended in April 2025. Waiting for a repealed section to act is how withholding defaults happen in transition years.

options.text: Nothing applies — goods purchases below ₹5 crore are outside withholding entirely
options.misconception: invents a threshold from the turnover test
options.why: Ten crore tests the buyer's size; fifty lakh tests the purchases per seller. Both are crossed, and no five-crore line exists anywhere in the section.

citation.ref: Section 194Q (TCS on goods omitted w.e.f. 1 April 2025)

items.scenario: In FY 2025-26 a manufacturer with ₹60 crore turnover buys ₹1.9 crore of steel from one resident supplier. Its accountant deducts nothing, reasoning that the seller will collect TCS on the sale as sellers always did, and that double taxation must be avoided.

items.stem: Is the full exemption right?

options.text: No — 54F works on net consideration, so investing ₹1.5 crore of ₹3 crore exempts only half the gain, ₹60 lakh
options.why: The adviser has computed section 54, which reinvests the gain — but that section is for selling a house. For shares, section 54F demands the net consideration be invested, exempting proportionately: 1.5/3 of the ₹1.2 crore gain, ₹60 lakh. The one existing house is within the not-more-than-one gate, so the claim survives — at half strength.

options.text: Yes, provided the shares' gain is otherwise taxable under section 112A
options.misconception: hangs the exemption on the levy section
options.why: 54F asks about the asset sold and the house bought, not which rate section would have taxed the gain. The proportionate formula still gives only ₹60 lakh.

options.text: Yes — a house costing more than the gain always absorbs it fully
options.misconception: applies section 54's gain-based formula to a 54F asset
options.why: The two sections' formulas differ by design: house-to-house asks the gain; anything-to-house asks the whole consideration, since otherwise sale proceeds could be enjoyed while a sliver bought exemption.

options.text: No exemption — owning any other house on the transfer date kills 54F
options.misconception: tightens the one-house gate to zero
options.why: The disqualification reads more than one residential house other than the new one. A single existing house is expressly tolerated.

items.scenario: An individual sells listed shares held six years for ₹3 crore (indexed cost irrelevant here; the long-term gain is ₹1.2 crore) and buys a residential flat for ₹1.5 crore. He owns one other house already. His adviser computes full exemption of the ₹1.2 crore gain since the flat's price exceeds the gain.

items.stem: What can an updated return do for him in June 2026?

options.text: Declare the omitted income with fifty per cent additional tax — but never the loss; an updated return cannot reduce liability
options.why: June 2026 sits in the second year after AY 2024-25's end, so the confession costs the tax and interest plus fifty per cent of them — the price of the second twelve months. The loss half of his hope is structurally barred: section 139(8A) refuses any updated return that shows a loss, lowers the liability, or raises a refund. The window's four-year reach (Finance Act 2025) changes when he may file, not what direction the numbers may move.

options.text: Both — an updated return replaces the original in full
options.misconception: treats ITR-U as a fresh return
options.why: It is a one-way instrument built to collect more tax with immunity from the worst consequences. Returns that cut both ways closed with the revised-return deadline.

options.text: Nothing — the window for AY 2024-25 shut twenty-four months after it ended
options.misconception: applies the pre-2025 window
options.why: The Finance Act 2025 stretched the window to forty-eight months, with the sixty and seventy per cent bands pricing the added years. AY 2024-25 remains open well past June 2026.

options.text: The income at twenty-five per cent additional tax, since he is volunteering
options.misconception: reads the first-year rate as the volunteer's rate
options.why: The bands run on the clock, not on virtue: twenty-five per cent belonged to the first twelve months, which ended in March 2026. His candour arrives in the fifty per cent band.

items.scenario: In June 2026 a consultant realises he omitted ₹18 lakh of foreign consulting receipts from his return for assessment year 2024-25. He also realises that including them converts his year into a small loss position on another business, and hopes an updated return can both confess the income and claim the loss, paying whatever surcharge applies.

items.stem: What is the correct ceiling, and does the ₹15 lakh survive?

options.text: Nothing — partner remuneration is never deductible, being profit distribution
options.misconception: states the pre-1993 world
options.why: Working partner remuneration within the ceiling is expressly deductible and taxed in the partners' hands instead. Total denial double-counts what the scheme deliberately splits.

options.text: ₹12.3 lakh on the old slabs, disallowing ₹2.7 lakh
options.misconception: applies the pre-2024 limits the accountant memorised
options.why: The old first-slab of three lakh and floor of ₹1.5 lakh were doubled. Stale limits under-allow by exactly the amendment Parliament passed.

options.text: ₹13.8 lakh — 90 per cent of the first ₹6 lakh plus 60 per cent of ₹14 lakh — so ₹1.2 lakh of the claim disallows
options.why: The Finance Act 2024 rewrote the slab from AY 2025-26: the first six lakh of book profit earns the higher of three lakh or ninety per cent (₹5.4 lakh here), and the remaining ₹14 lakh earns sixty per cent (₹8.4 lakh) — ₹13.8 lakh in all. The deed authorises ₹15 lakh, but the statute caps the deduction; the excess ₹1.2 lakh is disallowed in the firm's hands.

options.text: ₹15 lakh in full — the deed's authorisation is the only condition
options.misconception: reads the deed as the ceiling
options.why: The deed is the first gate; the statutory formula is the second. Remuneration beyond the formula is disallowed however solemnly the deed promises it.

items.scenario: For FY 2025-26 a firm's book profit is ₹20 lakh, and its deed authorises remuneration of ₹15 lakh to its two working partners, which the firm pays and claims. The accountant computes the deductible ceiling using the limits he memorised years ago: ₹1.5 lakh or 90 per cent on the first ₹3 lakh, and 60 per cent beyond.

items.stem: How do the write-off and the later recovery fare?

options.text: The write-off deducts on the book entry alone — irrecoverability need not be proved — and the ₹30 lakh is income of the year it arrives
options.why: Since the 1989 amendment the condition is that the debt is written off as irrecoverable in the accounts, not established as such — the Supreme Court settled that the officer cannot demand proof the debt died. The balancing safeguard is section 41(4): what returns is taxed when it returns, so the ₹30 lakh lands in the recovery year's income.

options.text: The disallowance stands — a live customer means a live debt
options.misconception: applies the pre-1989 establish-it-first test
options.why: That evidentiary battle is what the amendment ended. Commercial judgment recorded in the books carries the deduction; the recovery rule protects the revenue if the judgment proves pessimistic.

options.text: The write-off deducts, and the ₹30 lakh recovery is a tax-free windfall
options.misconception: takes the deduction and forgets its mirror
options.why: Section 41(4) exists precisely for this sequence. A deduction taken and cash later received without tax would make pessimistic write-offs a planning device.

options.text: The write-off deducts only after filing a recovery suit that fails
options.misconception: adds a litigation condition the section dropped
options.why: Requiring futile suits was the old regime's waste. The books' write-off is the statutory event; suing a hopeless debtor is commerce, not a tax condition.

items.scenario: A manufacturer writes off ₹90 lakh owed by a struggling customer, passing the entry before year-end. The assessing officer disallows it: the customer is still in business, recovery suits were never filed, and the debt might yet be paid. Two years later the customer, recovering, pays ₹30 lakh of the written-off amount.

items.stem: How does ICDS treat the two claims?

options.text: The contract loss deducts as prudence, the MTM waits as speculation
options.misconception: lets one anticipated loss through on sentiment
options.why: Prudence is the accounting reason for the provision — and anticipation of losses is exactly what the construction ICDS declines to import into tax.

options.text: Both wait — expected contract losses are not anticipated under ICDS, and speculative MTM losses are generally not deductible until settlement
options.why: Section 145(2)'s standards govern the computation whatever the books say: ICDS on construction contracts recognises losses as incurred by the percentage of completion, refusing the upfront ₹15 crore that Ind AS prudence demands; and ICDS I's general rule denies marked-to-market losses except where a specific ICDS allows them. The books stay Ind AS; the return adjusts both items out and reverses them over time.

options.text: Both deduct — audited accounts bind the assessing officer
options.misconception: promotes book profits into taxable profits
options.why: The computation standards exist precisely to detach tax from accounting prudence. Book-tax differences of this kind are the daily work of the computation.

options.text: Neither deducts ever — ICDS disallows provisions permanently
options.misconception: reads a timing standard as a prohibition
options.why: ICDS moves recognition, it does not extinguish it. The contract loss deducts as completion progresses, and the forward loss on settlement — later, not never.

items.scenario: A construction company's Ind AS accounts recognise a ₹15 crore provision for the expected total loss on an onerous contract in year one of three, and also book a ₹4 crore mark-to-market loss on open forward contracts held for a speculative position. The tax computation claims both, the CFO reasoning that audited Ind AS accounts are the last word for tax too.

items.stem: What does section 115BBC actually charge each?

options.text: Neither — donations to registered trusts are exempt income
options.misconception: lets registration absorb the anonymous-donation charge
options.why: Sections 11-12 exempt applied income; 115BBC carves anonymous receipts out of that comfort for secular trusts. Registration is the precondition of the regime, not immunity from this section.

options.text: The hospital pays 30 per cent on ₹55 lakh — the cushion of ₹25 lakh spares the rest — and the temple pays nothing under this section
options.why: The hospital's cushion is the higher of ₹1 lakh or 5 per cent of total donations (₹25 lakh), so ₹55 lakh of the anonymous ₹80 lakh bears the flat 30 per cent. The temple stands wholly outside: religious institutions' anonymous offerings are the section's express exception, Parliament recognising that hundi donations are anonymous by devotion, not design.

options.text: Both pay 30 per cent on their full anonymous receipts
options.misconception: misses both the cushion and the religious exception
options.why: The section's two mercies are its most examinable features. Charging the temple's hundi would tax a practice as old as the temples.

options.text: The hospital on ₹55 lakh, the temple on whatever exceeds its own ₹16 lakh cushion
options.misconception: gives the temple a cushion it does not need
options.why: The cushion mechanics never reach the temple — wholly religious institutions are excluded from the section before any computation begins.

items.scenario: A charitable hospital trust receives ₹5 crore of donations in the year, of which ₹80 lakh arrived in collection boxes with no donor records. Separately, a temple trust — wholly religious — counts ₹3 crore of anonymous hundi offerings. Both fear the 30 per cent anonymous-donation levy on their unrecorded receipts.

items.stem: What does section 35D actually allow?

options.text: ₹1.6 crore a year for five years — the full ₹8 crore amortised
options.misconception: spreads the whole spend and skips the five per cent cap
options.why: The cap is the section's binding constraint here: only ₹5 crore enters the amortisation at all. Instalments divide the capped pool, not the invoice total.

options.text: Nothing — preliminary expenses are permanently capital
options.misconception: states the pre-35D common law as the whole answer
options.why: That harsh default is real, and section 35D is its legislated exception for the listed expenses. Denying the ₹5 crore ignores the section outright.

options.text: ₹1 crore a year for five years — the pool caps at ₹5 crore (five per cent of the project), and the excess ₹3 crore earns nothing
options.why: Pre-commencement expenditure is capital in nature and undeducible but for this section, which rations its mercy twice: the qualifying pool cannot exceed five per cent of project cost — ₹5 crore here — and even that spreads over five equal instalments from commencement. The ₹3 crore beyond the cap simply perishes; neither this section nor section 37 rescues pre-business spending.

options.text: ₹8 crore in year one — expenses of starting up deduct when business starts
options.misconception: converts capital pre-commencement spending into revenue
options.why: Before the business exists there is no business to deduct against, which is the very gap 35D fills — on its own instalment and cap terms, not on the claimant's.

items.scenario: Before commencing its ₹100 crore plant, a company spends ₹8 crore on feasibility studies, project reports and incorporation-related legal work — all within the specified list. In year one of operations the CFO claims the entire ₹8 crore, calling it revenue expenditure of setting up.

items.stem: Where do you stand under Clause 8?

options.text: Not guilty — he communicated, and the outgoing auditor raised no objection
options.misconception: reads the clause as requiring communication in any form
options.why: Form is the substance here. A telephone call leaves nothing to show what was asked or answered, which is why the clause specifies writing.

options.text: Guilty, because the fee dispute meant he needed the outgoing auditor's consent
options.misconception: converts communication into permission
options.why: No consent is ever required — an outgoing auditor cannot veto a successor. Unpaid fees are a fact to weigh, not a bar. The failure is only the missing writing.

options.text: Guilty — the communication must be in writing, and a phone call is not that
options.why: The clause's words are "without first communicating with him in writing". The conversation happened and even produced no objection, but the safeguard the clause builds — a record that the incoming auditor asked and what he was told — exists only on paper. Oral communication, however cordial, is the misconduct.

options.text: Not guilty if he now sends a letter confirming the earlier call
options.misconception: backdates a safeguard that must come before acceptance
options.why: The clause says "first" — the writing must precede acceptance. A confirming letter after the appointment records the breach; it does not repair it.

items.scenario: A company removes its auditor and approaches you. You telephone the outgoing auditor, who says he has no objection but warns you the client disputes his fees. You accept the audit the next day, and a month later the outgoing auditor complains to the Institute that you never wrote to him.

items.stem: What may you tell the competitor client, and what must you give the tax officer?

options.text: Tell the competitor only what it could eventually learn from public filings
options.misconception: discloses early and calls it harmless
options.why: A pending negotiation is not public, and its value lies in the timing. What might become public later is still confidential now, and now is when you would be telling it.

options.text: Both — a firm owes each client the benefit of everything the firm knows
options.misconception: treats the firm's knowledge as a pooled asset of its clients
options.why: The information belongs to the engagement it came from. Pooling it is the precise disclosure the clause forbids, and would end professional confidence between auditor and client.

options.text: Nothing to the competitor; the summoned papers to the officer — legal compulsion is the exception, another client's interest is not
options.why: Clause 1 permits disclosure only with the client's consent or where law requires it. A statutory summons is the law requiring it. The competitor's commercial appetite is nothing at all — serving two clients does not merge their entitlement to what you learned from each.

options.text: Neither — auditor confidentiality is absolute, like privilege, and beats the summons
options.misconception: promotes a professional duty into a legal privilege
options.why: The clause itself carves out disclosure required by law. Defying a valid summons is not loyalty; it is contempt with a confidentiality label.

items.scenario: During an audit you discover your client is negotiating to buy a supplier. Another client of your firm competes with that supplier and would dearly want to know. Separately, an income-tax summons under section 131 requires you to produce the client's working papers.

items.stem: Does the disclosure save the engagement?

options.text: No — the clause bars the opinion itself where the firm or any partner has substantial interest, and disclosure is no cure
options.why: Clause 4 reaches "he, his firm, or a partner in his firm". One partner's 30 per cent poisons every signature the firm can produce, and the clause prohibits expressing the opinion — a prominent confession of the conflict still expresses it. Independence questions of this kind are answered by declining.

options.text: No, but the firm may accept if the partner undertakes to sell the shares within the year
options.misconception: audits first, becomes independent later
options.why: Independence is tested when the opinion is given. A promise to divest afterwards means the opinion was expressed while the interest stood — which is the whole offence.

options.text: Yes, provided the interested partner takes no part in the audit work
options.misconception: builds an information wall the clause does not recognise
options.why: The prohibition follows the interest, not the staffing chart. The firm profits from the fee and the partner from the company; no allocation of files changes either.

options.text: Yes — transparency lets the reader discount the opinion appropriately
options.misconception: substitutes disclosure for independence
options.why: Disclosure manages many things; this clause is not one of them. An opinion from an interested firm is worthless even when labelled, because the reader cannot un-know the auditor wanted a particular answer.

items.scenario: A two-partner firm is offered the audit of a private company in which one partner holds 30 per cent of the shares. The other partner proposes to sign the report personally, disclosing the shareholding prominently in the audit report so readers can weigh it.

items.stem: Is he guilty under Clause 7?

options.text: Yes — certifying without examination is gross negligence, and honesty is no defence to it
options.why: Clause 7 punishes the absence of due diligence, not the presence of dishonesty. A certificate tells the world the certifier verified; signing on the manager's say-so means he verified nothing. Good faith and a small fee measure his intentions, not his diligence.

options.text: No — reliance on management representations is an accepted audit technique
options.misconception: stretches a corroborating tool into a substitute for evidence
options.why: Representations support evidence; they never replace it. Where a certificate rests on nothing but the interested party's own statement, the technique has become the abdication.

options.text: No — without fraudulent intent there can be no professional misconduct
options.misconception: imports a mens rea requirement the clause deliberately omits
options.why: The Second Schedule separates dishonesty offences from negligence offences precisely so that careless certification is punishable on its own. Clause 7 is the negligence limb.

options.text: Yes, but only because the figures proved wrong — accurate figures would have cleared him
options.misconception: judges diligence by outcome
options.why: The breach was complete when he signed unverified. Figures that happened to be right would have been luck, and luck is not diligence.

items.scenario: A chartered accountant certifies the circulation figures of a newspaper for an advertising body, relying entirely on a statement prepared by the newspaper's manager, without checking the print orders, newsprint consumption, or dispatch records. The figures turn out inflated. He argues he acted honestly and charged a modest fee.

items.stem: Which engagements does Clause 11 permit?

options.text: None — a member in practice can hold no position in any company or business
options.misconception: erases the proviso and the permission routes
options.why: The clause's own proviso protects the plain board seat, and the Council's general permissions cover more. Absolute prohibition is the one reading the text itself contradicts.

options.text: Only the second — the trading partnership needs Council permission, and the auditor link poisons the third
options.why: Active business alongside practice is what the clause gates behind Council permission, and a working partnership in trade does not enjoy any general permission. A directorship simpliciter is saved by the proviso — but the proviso itself withdraws the saving where the member or any partner audits the company, which sinks the third.

options.text: All three — what a member does outside office hours is his own affair
options.misconception: reads professional exclusivity as a working-hours rule
options.why: The clause regulates occupation, not timetable. Divided commercial interests compromise independence at any hour, which is why permission is the Council's to give.

options.text: The second and third — directorships are always within the proviso
options.misconception: stops reading the proviso before its exception
options.why: The proviso saves directorship simpliciter "unless he or any of his partners is interested in such company as an auditor". The third scenario is that exception in terms.

items.scenario: A practising chartered accountant (1) joins his family's textile trading business as a working partner, without asking the Institute; (2) accepts an ordinary directorship in a listed company his firm does not audit; and (3) is offered a directorship in a company where his partner is the auditor.

items.stem: Is the CA guilty under Clause 10?

options.text: Yes, but only if the client account shortfall exceeded a reasonable float
options.misconception: invents a de minimis buffer the clause does not offer
options.why: The clause has no tolerance band. Separate account, intended use, reasonable time — each is absolute, and the salaries payment breached the second outright.

options.text: No — the tax was paid on time and the client lost nothing
options.misconception: measures the offence by the ending
options.why: The clause protects the arrangement, not just the outcome. A trustee who borrows the trust fund and wins is still a trustee who borrowed the trust fund.

options.text: No, because money handed voluntarily to a professional becomes his to manage
options.misconception: converts custody into ownership
options.why: The money was received for a stated purpose — that is custody. Fees belong to the firm; the client's tax money never did.

options.text: Yes, twice over — the money never entered a separate client account, and it was used for foreign purposes meanwhile
options.why: Money received to be expended for the client must sit in a separate banking account until spent as intended. The office account was the wrong pocket from day one, and paying salaries from it was use for a purpose never intended. Restoration and the punctual June deposit mitigate; they do not undo either limb.

items.scenario: A client hands a practising CA ₹12 lakh in March to deposit toward the client's advance tax in June. The CA parks the sum in the firm's office account, uses part of it through April to pay office salaries, restores the full amount in May, and deposits the tax on time in June. No fee remains unpaid and the client suffers no loss.

items.stem: Which of the three activities survive Clause 7?

options.text: None — any public mention of a CA's services breaches the clause
options.misconception: reads the clause without the Council's permissions
options.why: The B.Com may appear, and a compliant website may describe services. The line runs between being findable and being promoted, not between silence and speech.

options.text: All three — professionals may market like any other business today
options.misconception: assumes liberalisation that never reached the schedule
options.why: The clause still stands, guidelines and all. The profession's bargain is credibility for restraint; the Council loosened formats, not the principle.

options.text: Only the website — the card's claims and designations and the paid campaign are both misconduct
options.why: "Tax Guru and GST Specialist" are designations other than chartered accountant, and "fastest refunds" advertises services with self-praise — the card fails twice. A push campaign broadcasting an unbeaten record is advertisement in its plainest form. The website survives because it waits to be found — the pull basis the Council's guidelines permit — and states services without puffery.

options.text: The card and the website — printed cards are traditional and websites are modern practice
options.misconception: tests by medium instead of by content
options.why: The card's medium is fine; its designations and boasts are not. Clause 7 reads the words, not the paper they are printed on.

items.scenario: A practising CA prints visiting cards reading "CA R. Mehta, B.Com, Tax Guru and GST Specialist — fastest refunds in the city", runs a paid social media campaign promoting his firm's "unbeaten track record", and maintains a plain firm website describing services, which visitors find by searching.

items.stem: Which payments breach Clause 2?

options.text: None, provided each payment is disclosed in the firm's accounts
options.misconception: launders a prohibited outflow through transparency
options.why: Disclosure changes what is known, not what is allowed. A documented commission to a tout is a documented breach.

options.text: All three — professional fees can never be shared with anyone
options.misconception: reads the prohibition without its exceptions
options.why: The clause's list is half its text: partners, retired partners, their estates, fellow members, permitted professionals. Absolute bans on sharing would make partnership itself misconduct.

options.text: The widow's share and the agent's commission — only members may ever receive anything
options.misconception: shrinks the list to current members
options.why: The legal representative of a deceased partner is named in the clause itself. Firms could not honour succession arrangements otherwise.

options.text: Only the agent's commission — the widow and the fellow member are both within the clause's permitted list
options.why: The clause bars sharing fees with any person outside its list, and a referral commission to an insurance agent is its textbook breach — fees flowing to a non-member for procuring work. The deceased partner's legal representative is expressly permitted, honouring the firm's own bargain, and a member of the Institute was never outside the circle at all.

items.scenario: A practising CA makes three payments during the year: 10 per cent of audit fees to an insurance agent who steadily refers clients; a share of profits to the widow of a deceased partner under the partnership deed; and a referral share to a fellow chartered accountant who passed on an assignment too large for his own firm.

items.stem: How does the company account for the two amounts under Ind AS 115?

options.text: Capitalise both as contract cost assets and amortise over the pattern of transfer of the related goods or services
options.why: The ₹2 lakh commission is an incremental cost of obtaining the contract — it would not have been incurred without winning the deal — and is recoverable, so para 91 capitalises it absent the one-year practical expedient. The ₹8 lakh set-up cost relates directly to this contract, creates a resource used to satisfy the performance obligations, and is expected to be recovered, meeting all three para 95 conditions for a fulfilment cost asset. Both amortise consistently with the transfer of the goods or services to which the asset relates.

options.text: Capitalise only the set-up cost, and expense the commission because sales commissions are always a selling expense
options.misconception: assumes commissions can never meet the incremental-cost test
options.why: A sales commission earned only on winning the contract is the standard's own example of an incremental cost of obtaining a contract. It is capitalised when recovery is expected, unless the practical expedient applies.

options.text: Expense both immediately, because contract-related costs are always period costs
options.misconception: ignores the two dedicated capitalisation gateways Ind AS 115 provides for contract costs
options.why: Ind AS 115 carves out both cost types from being automatically expensed — the commission meets the incremental-cost test and the set-up spend meets the three fulfilment-cost conditions, so neither is a blanket period cost.

options.text: Capitalise only the commission, and expense the set-up cost as general administrative overhead
options.misconception: treats a contract-specific asset build as an unallocated overhead
options.why: The set-up cost is not general overhead — it relates directly to this one contract, generates a resource, the database, that the entity uses to satisfy performance obligations, and is recoverable. That is exactly what para 95 capitalises.

items.scenario: A company pays its sales staff a commission of ₹2 lakh for winning a three-year service contract. Separately, before mobilising its team onto the contract, the company incurs ₹8 lakh in set-up costs that build a customised database used only to deliver that contract's services and are expected to be recovered through the contract price.

items.stem: Can the company apply hedge accounting to this forward contract from inception?

options.text: No — documentation of the risk management objective and strategy must exist at hedge inception, not be prepared afterwards
options.why: Para 6.4.1 requires formal designation and documentation at the inception of the hedging relationship, covering the risk management objective and strategy, the hedging instrument, the hedged item, the nature of the risk hedged and how effectiveness will be assessed. Documentation created after part of the hedged transaction has already occurred fails this condition, so hedge accounting is not available for the relationship as designated.

options.text: No, because forecast transactions can never be hedged items under Ind AS 109
options.misconception: forgets that a highly probable forecast transaction is an eligible hedged item
options.why: A highly probable forecast transaction is expressly an eligible hedged item for a cash flow hedge. The problem here is the late documentation, not the nature of the hedged item.

options.text: Yes, provided the hedge turns out to be effective by year end
options.misconception: substitutes a retrospective effectiveness outcome for the inception documentation requirement
options.why: Effectiveness is assessed on an ongoing basis, but it does not cure a missing inception-date designation. The documentation condition is tested at the start of the relationship, not inferred from the eventual result.

options.text: Yes, because the forward contract and the forecast sale are both real economic exposures
options.misconception: treats economic substance alone as sufficient, ignoring the formal documentation gateway
options.why: An economic relationship is necessary but not sufficient. Ind AS 109 additionally requires contemporaneous formal documentation; a real hedge without it does not qualify for hedge accounting.

items.scenario: A company enters a forward contract to hedge highly probable forecast export sales six months ahead. It designates the hedge and prepares a note the following month, after part of the forecast sale has already been recognised, describing the hedged risk and how effectiveness will be assessed.

items.stem: How does the company account for the transfer under Ind AS 109?

options.text: Continue to recognise the loans in full and recognise a financial liability for the proceeds received
options.why: A guarantee reimbursing the transferee for substantially all default losses on the full portfolio means the seller has substantially retained the risks and rewards of ownership. Para 3.2.6 requires the asset to continue to be recognised in its entirety, with the consideration received treated as a financial liability, not a sale.

options.text: Derecognise the loans in full, because legal title has passed to the bank
options.misconception: treats legal transfer of title as sufficient for derecognition
options.why: Ind AS 109 looks past legal form to the transfer of risks and rewards. Title can pass while credit risk is substantially retained through a guarantee, which blocks derecognition regardless of the legal sale.

options.text: Derecognise the loans and recognise a contingent liability only if an outflow becomes probable
options.misconception: confuses a retained financial guarantee within a transfer with an Ind AS 37 contingent liability
options.why: This guarantee is part of assessing whether the transfer itself qualifies for derecognition under Ind AS 109, not a separate contingent liability judged later under Ind AS 37. Because it retains substantially all the risk, the transfer fails derecognition from the outset.

options.text: Derecognise the loans and separately recognise a guarantee liability at fair value
options.misconception: applies the partial risks-and-rewards or continuing-involvement treatment to a case of substantial retention
options.why: That treatment applies when the entity neither substantially transfers nor substantially retains risks and rewards, so a control test decides the outcome. Full retention through a guarantee covering the whole portfolio is decided by the risks-and-rewards test alone, with no derecognition.

items.scenario: A company sells a portfolio of fixed-rate loans to a bank at their carrying amount but retains a guarantee obligation reimbursing the bank for the full amount of any default, capped at the entire value of the portfolio, for the loans' remaining life.

items.stem: What deferred tax effect does the acquirer recognise, and what happens to goodwill?

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹5 crore, which increases goodwill by ₹5 crore to ₹65 crore
options.why: The fair-valued trademark creates a taxable temporary difference of ₹20 crore against its unchanged tax base. Para 19 requires the resulting deferred tax liability to be recognised as an identifiable liability in the acquisition accounting, and because it was not separately priced into the consideration, it feeds into goodwill — raising it by the same ₹5 crore.

options.text: No deferred tax effect, because the initial recognition exemption in Ind AS 12 blocks it
options.misconception: applies the goodwill initial-recognition exemption to an unrelated identifiable asset
options.why: The initial recognition exemption is specifically for goodwill itself, precisely so deferred tax does not spiral by inflating goodwill on goodwill. It does not extend to other identifiable assets recognised in the same combination, which get full deferred tax treatment.

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹5 crore recognised directly in equity, leaving goodwill at ₹60 crore
options.misconception: routes an acquisition-accounting deferred tax item through equity instead of the acquisition
options.why: This deferred tax liability arises from the acquisition itself, not from an item the entity recognised outside profit or loss. Para 19 puts it inside the acquisition accounting, which is exactly what moves goodwill.

options.text: A deferred tax asset of ₹5 crore, reducing goodwill to ₹55 crore
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the temporary difference on an asset revalued upward
options.why: Revaluing the trademark upward without a matching tax base increase creates a taxable, not deductible, temporary difference — the asset will generate more taxable income than its tax base allows for, which is a liability, not an asset.

items.scenario: On acquiring a subsidiary, the acquirer fair values an identifiable trademark at ₹20 crore above its tax base, with a tax rate of 25 per cent applying to the future reversal. Goodwill before considering this item is ₹60 crore.

items.stem: Where does this exchange loss appear in the group's consolidated financial statements?

options.text: Eliminated entirely on consolidation, as an intragroup balance
options.misconception: treats a net-investment loan the same as an ordinary intragroup balance due for elimination
options.why: A genuine intragroup loan is eliminated in full because it is an internal balance the group as a whole never owed. This loan's exchange difference is a real economic effect of currency movement on a real net investment, so it is not eliminated — it is reclassified to OCI instead.

options.text: In other comprehensive income, and it stays there until the net investment is disposed of
options.why: A loan whose settlement is neither planned nor likely is, in substance, part of the net investment in the foreign operation. Para 32 identifies it as such, and para 48 recognises the resulting exchange difference in OCI within the consolidated statements, reclassifying it to profit or loss only when the net investment is disposed of.

options.text: In profit or loss, because all monetary item exchange differences flow through profit or loss
options.misconception: applies the ordinary monetary-item rule while ignoring the net-investment exception the consolidated statements carry
options.why: That is the treatment in the parent's own separate financial statements. In the consolidated statements that include the foreign operation, the same exchange difference is redirected to OCI precisely because it relates to a balance the group has decided, in substance, not to settle.

options.text: Split between profit or loss and OCI in proportion to the loan's currency exposure
options.misconception: invents an apportionment the standard does not provide
options.why: Ind AS 21 does not split this exchange difference. Once a monetary item is identified as part of the net investment, its exchange difference goes to OCI in full in the consolidated statements.

items.scenario: A parent has advanced a long-term loan to its foreign subsidiary that neither party plans to settle in the foreseeable future — in substance an extension of the parent's investment. In the current year the loan generates an exchange loss of ₹3 crore.

items.stem: What gain does the seller-lessee recognise on the transaction?

options.text: The full ₹4 crore gain, deferred and released to profit or loss over the eight-year leaseback term
options.misconception: imports the pre-Ind AS 116 deferred-gain approach that the current sale-and-leaseback model replaced
options.why: Ind AS 116 does not defer and amortise a sale-leaseback gain over the lease term. It instead recognises immediately only the portion of gain relating to the rights transferred, determined at the transaction date.

options.text: Only the gain relating to the 30 per cent of rights transferred to the buyer-lessor, not the full ₹4 crore
options.why: Because the transfer qualifies as a sale under the Ind AS 115 test, para 100 caps the seller-lessee's recognised gain to the portion relating to the rights actually transferred. The right-of-use asset retained is measured at 70 per cent of the ₹6 crore carrying amount, so only the gain attributable to the 30 per cent of rights sold reaches profit or loss — the rest stays unrecognised, embedded in the carrying amount of the retained right-of-use asset.

options.text: The full ₹4 crore gain, since the sale proceeds equal fair value
options.misconception: treats sale-leaseback gain the same as an outright sale with no leaseback
options.why: An outright sale with no continuing interest recognises the whole gain. Here the seller-lessee keeps using the asset for eight more years through the leaseback, so para 100 only lets through the gain on the rights genuinely transferred, not the rights it continues to hold through the right-of-use asset.

options.text: No gain at all, because the seller-lessee continues to occupy the property
options.misconception: assumes any continued occupation defeats sale accounting entirely
options.why: Continued occupation through a leaseback does not by itself block sale accounting — the Ind AS 115 control test decides that. Once the transfer passes that test, a partial gain is recognised; it is not suppressed to zero merely because a leaseback exists.

items.scenario: A company sells a warehouse it owns for ₹10 crore cash — its fair value — when its carrying amount is ₹6 crore, and immediately leases it back for eight of the warehouse's remaining ten years. The transfer meets the Ind AS 115 conditions to be accounted for as a sale, and the right of use retained is measured at 70 per cent of the previous carrying amount.

items.stem: Does this timing comply with Ind AS 36?

options.text: No — the unit carrying the newly acquired goodwill must be tested before the end of the current annual period, not wait for the next annual test date
options.why: Para 96 makes an exception for goodwill acquired during the current annual period — the unit it sits in must be tested for impairment before that period ends, precisely so freshly acquired goodwill is not carried untested through an entire year before its first check.

options.text: Yes, because Ind AS 36 only requires each unit to be tested once every twelve months from when goodwill was allocated to it
options.misconception: applies a rolling twelve-month rule instead of the current-period cutoff for newly acquired goodwill
options.why: The general rule lets different units be tested at different times each year, but para 96 overrides that for goodwill acquired in the current period — that unit's first test cannot be pushed past the end of the same annual period.

options.text: Yes, provided the entity discloses the different test date for the new unit in its notes
options.misconception: treats disclosure as a substitute for meeting the current-period testing deadline
options.why: Disclosure does not cure a test performed after the deadline the standard itself sets for newly acquired goodwill. The unit must actually be tested before the current annual period ends.

options.text: No, because all units with goodwill must be tested on the same date within an entity
options.misconception: assumes a single test date applies entity-wide
options.why: Ind AS 36 expressly allows different units to be tested at different times, provided each unit is tested at the same time every year. The problem here is not a mismatch between units — it is testing the new unit too late for the year the goodwill was acquired.

items.scenario: A company tests two of its cash-generating units for goodwill impairment every 30 September, in line with its policy. It acquires a third business, allocates goodwill to a new cash-generating unit on 1 January, and plans to first test that unit on the following 30 September, in line with the same policy.

items.stem: How does the company treat the stock options in computing diluted EPS?

options.text: Average the two incremental EPS figures and include both at the blended rate
options.misconception: invents an averaging mechanism the standard does not use
options.why: Ind AS 33 tests dilution issue by issue against basic EPS, not by blending incremental rates across instruments. An antidilutive issue is dropped entirely from the computation, not averaged into a lower combined rate.

options.text: Exclude the options from diluted EPS, because their incremental EPS of ₹14 exceeds basic EPS of ₹10, making them antidilutive
options.why: A potential equity share is antidilutive when including it would increase EPS rather than decrease it. Here the options' incremental effect of ₹14 per share is above the ₹10 basic EPS, so folding them in would raise EPS, not dilute it. Para 41 excludes antidilutive potential equity shares from the diluted EPS computation; the debentures, at ₹6 incremental EPS, are dilutive and are included.

options.text: Include the options along with the debentures, because diluted EPS must reflect every outstanding potential equity share
options.misconception: assumes diluted EPS includes all potential equity shares regardless of effect
options.why: Diluted EPS is not simply every potential share included. Para 41 specifically strips out any issue whose inclusion would be antidilutive, which is exactly the case for these options.

options.text: Include the options but exclude the debentures, because options are always included ahead of convertible instruments
options.misconception: invents a priority by instrument type instead of testing each by its dilutive effect
options.why: Ind AS 33 has no such hierarchy by instrument type. Each issue is tested on its own incremental EPS effect — the debentures qualify because they are dilutive at ₹6, and the options are excluded because they are antidilutive at ₹14, regardless of which instrument is which.

items.scenario: A company's basic EPS for the year is ₹10. It has outstanding convertible debentures that, if converted, would add ₹1,20,000 to profit (net of tax) and 20,000 shares to the weighted average count, an incremental EPS of ₹6 per additional share. It also has stock options that, if exercised, would add shares at an incremental EPS of ₹14 per additional share.

items.stem: How is the claim treated in each of the two years?

options.text: Recognised as an asset in year one and reversed through profit or loss if the appeal had succeeded
options.misconception: recognises on a probable outcome and treats reversal as the normal mechanism instead of never recognising a merely probable inflow
options.why: Ind AS 37 does not recognise a merely probable contingent asset and plan to reverse it later. It withholds recognition until virtual certainty is reached, which avoids exactly this risk of booking and unwinding an asset.

options.text: Recognised as an asset in year one, because winning the lower court claim is a favourable event
options.misconception: recognises on the strength of the initial win, ignoring that the outcome remains contested on appeal
options.why: A pending appeal keeps the outcome short of virtually certain. Para 33 bars recognition of a contingent asset at that stage regardless of the initial favourable ruling, precisely to avoid booking income the appeal could still reverse.

options.text: Disclosed as a contingent asset in year one, then recognised as an asset and income in year two
options.why: In year one, recovery is probable but not virtually certain, so para 34 calls for disclosure rather than recognition — recognising it would risk booking income that might not materialise. In year two, the appeal's withdrawal makes recovery virtually certain, so para 35 requires the asset and the related income to be recognised in that period, since it is no longer contingent.

options.text: Not disclosed or recognised in either year, because contingent assets are always kept out of the financial statements
options.misconception: treats the recognition bar as if it also barred disclosure
options.why: The recognition bar in para 33 is not a disclosure bar. Once an inflow is probable, para 34 requires disclosure even though recognition is still withheld — that is exactly year one here.

items.scenario: A company has filed and won a lower-court claim for damages against a supplier. The supplier has appealed, and legal counsel advises that the appeal has a low chance of succeeding, making recovery probable but not virtually certain. At the following year end, the appeal is withdrawn and the amount becomes virtually certain to be received.

items.stem: What does the company recognise in year two?

options.text: No change, because the fair value at grant date is locked in for the whole vesting period
options.misconception: applies the equity-settled grant-date freeze to a cash-settled award
options.why: Grant-date measurement that is never remeasured is the equity-settled treatment. A cash-settled award is explicitly the opposite case — its liability is fair-valued afresh at every reporting date until settlement.

options.text: A decrease in the liability to ₹25 lakh, with the ₹15 lakh reduction credited to profit or loss
options.why: Cash-settled awards are remeasured to fair value at every reporting date under para 33, with the change taken to profit or loss. A fall in the underlying share price reduces the liability's fair value, and the entity recognises that fall as income (or a reduced expense) in year two — the reverse of an equity-settled award, which is never remeasured for share price movements at all.

options.text: The liability stays at ₹40 lakh, and the ₹15 lakh difference is disclosed only in the notes as a contingent gain
options.misconception: defers a required remeasurement to disclosure instead of recognising it
options.why: Para 33 requires the liability itself to be remeasured on the face of the financial statements, with the movement in profit or loss. This is not a matter left to note disclosure.

options.text: The liability is reduced to ₹25 lakh, with the ₹15 lakh adjustment taken directly to equity
options.misconception: routes a cash-settled remeasurement through equity instead of profit or loss
options.why: Equity-settled awards can involve an equity credit, but a cash-settled award's liability remeasurement always runs through profit or loss, because the entity has an obligation to pay cash, not to issue its own equity instruments.

items.scenario: A company grants employees cash-settled share appreciation rights. At the end of year one, the fair value of the liability recognised is ₹40 lakh. By the end of year two, before any rights are exercised, the fair value of the liability has fallen to ₹25 lakh because the share price dropped.

items.stem: How should the financial statements be prepared and what, if anything, is disclosed?

options.text: Prepared on a break-up basis, because any covenant breach automatically triggers liquidation accounting
options.misconception: treats an unresolved covenant breach as itself an intention or necessity to liquidate
options.why: A break-up basis is only required when management actually intends to liquidate or cease trading, or has no realistic alternative. An unresolved covenant breach with ongoing negotiations and management's genuine belief in continuation does not, by itself, force that conclusion.

options.text: Disclosure is optional, left to management's judgement about materiality to users
options.misconception: treats a mandatory disclosure trigger as discretionary once judged material
options.why: Once management judges the uncertainty material enough to cast significant doubt on going concern, para 25 requires its disclosure — it is not an optional add-on once that threshold is crossed.

options.text: Prepared on a going concern basis with no disclosure, since management is confident the negotiations will succeed
options.misconception: lets management's own confidence substitute for disclosing an unresolved material uncertainty
options.why: Confidence about the outcome does not remove the uncertainty that exists at the reporting date — the waiver has not been obtained. Para 25 requires disclosure of material uncertainties management is aware of, whatever management privately expects the outcome to be.

options.text: Prepared on a going concern basis, with the material uncertainty around the covenant breach and negotiations disclosed
options.why: Management has no intention to liquidate and no realistic alternative but to continue, so para 25 keeps the going concern basis. But the unresolved covenant breach casts significant doubt on that ability, so the material uncertainty itself is disclosed — the standard's mechanism for exactly this situation, short of actually abandoning the going concern basis.

items.scenario: A company has breached a loan covenant, and its bank has not yet waived the breach as of the date the financial statements are approved. Management believes, based on ongoing negotiations, that the entity will continue operating for the foreseeable future, and has no intention or need to liquidate or cease trading.

items.stem: How does the company correct this in the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: Treat it as a change in accounting estimate and adjust prospectively from 1 April 2025
options.misconception: recharacterises a computational error using the wrong useful life as an estimate change
options.why: Using the wrong useful life in the calculation is an error, not a reassessment of an estimate based on new information. Ind AS 8 corrects errors retrospectively; only a genuine change in estimate is applied prospectively.

options.text: Charge the ₹1.5 crore against profit or loss for the year ended 31 March 2026, as a prior period item within current-year income
options.misconception: treats retrospective correction as a current-period catch-up charge
options.why: Routing the correction through the current year's profit or loss is exactly what para 46 excludes. The error belongs to 2025 and is corrected there, by restatement, leaving 2026's own result untouched by it.

options.text: Restate the comparative figures for the year ended 31 March 2025 as if the correct useful life had always been used, with no effect on the current year's profit or loss
options.why: Para 42 corrects a material prior period error retrospectively by restating the comparative amounts for the period in which it occurred. Para 46 keeps that correction out of the current period's profit or loss — the ₹1.5 crore overstatement is fixed in the 2025 comparative column, not charged against 2026's results.

options.text: Leave the 2025 comparative figures unchanged and disclose the error only in the notes, since it relates to a closed prior year
options.misconception: substitutes note disclosure for the required restatement of the affected period
